Dynamite Explosions Cause Alarm. Some person or persons unknown have been using dynamite recently about the village of Texas, N. C. R. R., causing considerable anxiety among residents. Two explosions have occurred thus far, one on Tuesday evening about 8.30 o'clock and the other about 2 o'clock Wednesday morning. The first went off at a stone house occupied by Arch Wye, colored. The dynamite had been placed at the sill of one of the doors. The building shook and the inmates were greatly alarmed. The early morning explosion was near the Bosley lime kilns, where men were engaged in attending the kilns. They were greatly excited. The damage was slight at both places. It is said exception is taken to the colored and some foreign laborers coming to work about the quarries, and the explosions are to intimidate them. The reports were heard for a considerable distance from the village.

IS THIS WHAT WE ARE TO GET UNDER THE NEW DEMOCRATIC ADMINISTRATION?
"The Fight That The Demcrats Made Under The Head of Negro Domination" Bearing Fruit The Masonic Temple on Courtland Street Stoned By A Mob Of White Boys And Men Members Going Into The Building Are Greeted With Stones, Tin Cans and Shouts of Nigger."-Policeman In No Burry To Get To The Place.

One of the most disgraceful things seen in this city since the days of "Ping Ulyssim" was the stoning of the Mausone Temple on Courtland street, on Tesday night. A large bon-fire had been built on the corner of Pleasant and Courtland streets, and there were a howling mob of boys and men surrounding it. They were having their own fun and piling high dry goods boxes and other material on the fire, when it occurred to some of them that they might get a little more fun out of the situation. Members of one of the Lodges commenced to make their appearance on the scene making their way to the Temple. Several stones were thrown, but as they hit no one no attention was paid to it, little thinking what was to be outcome. Not meeting with any resistance, about nine e'clock, white the members were quietly engaged with their business, they were startled by a crash of broken glass, quickly followed by another and another. This annoted the members, and calling off the work of the Lodge, the members piled out into the street threatening vengeance on the heads of the miscreants. Hardly had they made their appearance when they were met with a volley of stones. This of course enraged them and they made for the howling mob of upwards of two hundred white men and boys. It is needless to say that there was a scattering of the crowd, and as the colored men made their way further up the street, more stones were thrown and one or two pistol shots were fired. Happily no one was injured by them. Had any one of the shots taken effect, it is hard to say what would have happened because the men were enraged by the dastardly attack upon them and their Temple.
baltimore-baltimore-1903-11-03.A2:
Several of the members hurried to the Central Police Station and demanded protection. There were but few policemen present, and those in authority told the men to go back to their hall and protection would be sent them. After persistent effort, a single policeman was sent with the men, and he took his time in getting up to the place, saying: "I have been on my feet all day and I am tired, and don't feel like being bothered." The men urged but, he simply declined to do any hurry. When he arrived on the scene, the mob was pretty well scattered, fearing the vengeance of the colored men who were standing around their hall.

They finally went back to their business and there was no more trouble. The persistent fight that has been made on the Negro during the past few weeks have embolized the white toughs, and the Negro has trouble coming to him. The School Board has taken the matter under consideration.

baltimore-baltimore-1903-11-03.A3:
A TASTE OF MOB VIOLENCE
One of the most dastardly outrages ever known in this city was the riddling of the front of the colored Masonic Temple, on Courtland street, on Tuesday night and Wednesday morning. A huge bon-fire had been built on the corner of Pleas ant and Courtland Streets, and surrounded by a howling mob of boys and young men, while the streets in the vicinity were lined with people on their doorsteps and in windows looking at the firs. As the hour of meeting approached several members of Enterprise Lodge No. 3, whose meeting night it was, came down the street, and as they neared the building, were fired upon with stones. They were, however, not much alarmed, nor gave the matter much attention, attributing it to the usual outburst after almost every election. When, however, an hour after, they found that their building was being stoned, the matter proved more serious. Not satisfied with breaking a number of windows on Tuesday night, they returned on Wednesday morning and completed the work os destruction. Hardly a pane of glass remains in the front of the building, which is a three story one. One of the worse features of the matter was the utter indifference of the police department, it being almost impossible to get a policeman to the scene of the disturbance, although several members of the Lodge went to the police station in person, and asked for protection. Nobody in the city ever remembers such a thing as happening before. There have been elections in which colored people have been driven from the polls and even beaten and shot, but there was no destruction of property, and the colored people have owned property in this state for many years past, even in the days of slavery. Tue whole thing was the outcome of the bitter partisan attack for political purposes by the speakers for the democratic ticket. Such things have a tendency to give the mob to believe that they can do as they please, and they are not always discriminating enough to know that the whole thing is for effect and done in order to carry the election against the other party. However, there is no justification of such a dastardly deed, and if the miscreants are caught they will, no doubt receive the full penalty of the law. One thing is assured, that every effort will be put forth
and done in order to carry the election against the other party. However, there is no justification of such a dastardly deed, and if the miscreants are caught they will, no doubt receive the full penalty of the law. Mr. William E. Tilghman Arrested On The Word Of A Street Car Conductor---Grand Jury Dismisses The Case--Mr. Tilghman Called In And Heard

The aftermath in the late election seems to manifest itself in perpetrating outrages upon respectable colored citizens all over the city. From the fact that the Democrats carried the election, many of the lower class of whites seem to think that they can do as they please when it comes to the colored people. A conductor on the Pennsylvania line of the United Railway company was assaulted on last Saturday evening by a colored man, so he said, and the man escaped. On Wednesday, after the outrage upon the Masonic Temple Courtland street, Mr. Tilghman, who is the Grand Master of Masons (colored) of this State, started to go to the Marshal's office to see him in reference to the matter. He boarded a Pennsylvania avenue car at Dolphin street, paid his fare and had rode to the corner of Baltimore and Greene streets, when the car came to a sudden stop. The car going in the opposite direction also came to a sudden stop, which caused the passengers of both cars to wonder what had happened. It seems that the conductor of the car on which Mr. Tilghman was riding saw a policeman, and hailed him and ordered the arrest of Mr. Tilghman asked the conductor if he had not paid his fare. The conductor replied that he had, sometime ago. When Mr. Tilghman inquired why the policeman arrested him, he was told that he would find cut when he got to the police station.

Business Is Tied Up. New Orleans: The screwmen's and longshoremen's strike has effectually tied up the cotton export business on the river front, and there is no immediate prospect of a settlement of the trouble. The ship agents and the strikers are stubborn and neither side shows an inclination to yield. In the meantime, cotton is being diverted to Galveston, Mobile, Pensacola and other cities, and the business of the port is suffering. Several steamships bound for New Orleans have been ordered to other ports to receive their cargoes. The cotton exchange attempted to effect a settlement of the controversy, but failed, and now the board of trade will try its hand. The Big Rice Company.
Crowley, La.: There no longer seems any doubt but that a movement is on foot for the purpose of a mam-moth rice company to operate on Louisiana and Texas rice. A well known rice man stated yesterday that the movement was backed by Chicago capital and that the deal is soon to be made public. It is said that the deal is meeting with favor among the rice milers, who, it is understood, are to co-operate with the promoters of the new company.

Trying for a Settlement.

Trying for a Settlement.

New Orleans, La.: The board of trade late last night addressed a communication to the different commercial bodies in New Orleans calling a meeting for this afternoon for the purpose of devising a plan to settle the screwmen's strike. The communication recites that commerce is being driven away from New Orleans to other ports and that the time for definite and positive action has arrived.

No Settlement in Sight.

No Settlement in Sight.

New Orlaesn, La.: The mediation committee of the cotton exchange, which has been wrestling with the problem of peaceably settling the differences between the screwmen and the ship agents, made a final report to the directors of the exchange yesterday afternoon, which was accepted. The committee is now discharged. All negotiations looking toward a settlement of the trouble have been declared off.

American Firms Suffered.

New Orleans, La.: A cablegram from Bluefields, Nicaragua, says a large section of the business district of that city was destroyed by fire last night. Several American firms suffered heavy losses.

Rain in Southern Louisiana.

Crowley, La.: The rain that fell early this morning was general over Southern Louisiana and will prove worth many thousands of dollars to the rice crop. Reports from Gueydan, Jennings, Eunice, Rayne and Estherwood are to the effect that the rain fell in those sections.

Texas Is Represented.

New Orleans: Texas is very much in evidence at the national convention of the American Medical Association, and scores of prominent physicians from the Lone Star state are in the city. The state has been given a prominent place on the program, and three physicians from that commonwealth will read papers.

Negroes Threatened.

Beaumont, Texas: Yesterday morning when the men went to work at the refineries in the South End they found a notice posted at the refineries to the effect that the negroes must leave the place at once or (skull and bones), and with the explanation below: "You know what that means."

German Landowners to Make a Tour. Washington: The party of German landowners and experts in agriculture who are to make a tour of the United States spent the day in Washington sightseeing. They will remain here until Tuesday, when they leave for the West, stopping first at Martinsburg, W. Va., where a fruit nursery will be visited. Mr. J. L. Schulte, as the chief of the department of agriculture, will accompany the Germans on their tour.

THE SEVENTH WONDER OF THE WORLD.
The advance sheets of this somewhat startling publication have reached this office. Its author, Mr. B. N. Boyd, of Greenville, North Carolina, who has already acquired some reputation as a landscape gardener in his own and adjacent states has ventured into literature with the determination to establish his theory that the Negro was the original man, that Adam was the color of the soil, and that the white or composite races are an evolution. Sacred and profane history have both been appealed to in support of his contention, and with what result it requires a perusal of the volume to determine

Mr. Boyd is quite familiar with the terminology of scientific works and less surprising is his comprehension of biblical text and concordance. The work is unique and its readers will doubtless experience various emotions. We anticipate for it an immense sale.

RACE WAR IN CINCINNATI.
White Men Defend White Women from Insults of Negroes. Cincinnati, O.. Nov. 25. -A race war
Insults of Negroes.
Cincinnati, O., Nov. 25.—A race war that terminated in one white man be-stabbed nearly to death and three negroes narrowly escaping being mobbed, occurred in the center of this city early yesterday morning.
Two white women, who escaped in the melee, were standing at Sixth and Vine streets, when three negroes came up, and as no one was about at that time, began to insult the women. White men were soon on the scene and in a few minutes a crowd had gathered, and made a rush for the negroes.
John McCarthy, one of the white men
cincinnati-cincinnati-1903-12.A2: was stabbed three times and may die. The negroes were roughly handled, and it was only the quick work of the police that prevented them from being killed.

Pittsburg—Former Postmaster Colonel Nathaniel P. Sawyer, aged 74, banker, manufacturer, politician and friend of President Andrew Johnson, died yesterday.

Pittsburg—Senator Foraker, here for the Chamber of Commerce banquet, said Roosevelt will be nominated without opposition and re-elected president.

Chicago—Mayor Harrison declares the city will enter the electric lighting field in competition with the gas trust.

St. Louis—Three men were fatally hurt at the Union Syrup company's plant. Employees say the floor collapsed. The police declare the boiler exploded.

Detroit, Mich.—Minority stockholders seek to set aside the forced sale of the Michigan Telephone company, alleging fraud to freeze them out.

Boston—Charles Dupee Blake, author of "Rock a Bye Baby" and other songs, died at his home here, aged 60 years.

Boston—General John C. Black, commander-in-chief of the G. A. R., announces the next annual encampment will commence here Aug. 15.

Williamstown, Mass.—One new case of typhoid fever was reported yesterday in the village, but so far as can be learned it has no connection with the cases among the Williams college students.

Providence, R. I.—Brown university's typhoid fever alarm is over. No fear of new cases is felt and encouraging reports come from the sick students in the Rock Island hospital.

Elmira N. Y.—There have been sixty-four cases of typhoid at the New York state reformatory and four deaths from the disease.

Indianapolis—Charles and Ophelia Duhme of Cincinnati are charged with recklessness and waste in the management of the estate of the demented young millionaire, Frederick Chase, in an action for an accounting.

Cincinnati—Three negroes insulted two white women in the center of the city. A riot ensued. John McCarthy, a white man, was tabbed three times and the negroes were saved from death by the police.

New York—Judge Lacomb refused the application of the heirs of the late Richard Wagner for an injunction to restrain the production of Parsifal by Heinrich Conreid.

Leonard Wood's nomination as major general is likely to be reported favorably by the committee, but opposition will be continued.

Harry Hooper of Fairmount (Ind.), is surrounded in thicket by 200 armed men after killing Marshal Payne, who arrested him for burglary.

Most of the 200 employes at the United States Zinc and Chemical company's plant at Argentine, Kan., struck because of a cut in wages.

Nearly 300 policemen were detailed by Commissioner Green of New York to guard President Roosevelt when he attended the funeral of J. K. Gracie.

Twelve hundred employes of the Henry Lomb, Rochester (N. Y.) optical goods maker, were presented with bank accounts, proportioned to their wages.

Ira Curtis, a sawyer, was nearly cut in two at Anderson Brothers' sawmill near Harrisburg, Ill. He cannot recover. He is 40 years of age and has a family.

Brown university's typhoid fever alarm is over. No fear of new cases is felt and encouraging reports come from the sick students in the Rock Island hospital.

Four firemen were burned to death at Omaha and property loss of $300,000 was inflicted by a fire in Allen Bros'. wholesale grocery, and Pacific storage building.

In New York Judge Lacomb refused the application of the heirs of the late Richard Wagner for an injunction to restrain the production of Parsifal by Heinrich Conreid.

President Roosevelt's re-election is made practically certain by the increasing list of sure republican states; 227 of the needed 239 electoral votes are beyond doubt.

Three sailors on the German ship Octavia were killed by drinking carbolic acid, which the ship's sailmaker is accused of giving them for whisky, in spite.

Charged with coloring oleomargarine and selling it for country butter, R. M. Dockum, a prominent grocer at Springfield, Ill., was held to the federal grand jury.

W. J. Bryan was a guest of honor at a luncheon given in London by Ambassador Choate. Premier Balfour, Ritchie, Sir Clinton Dawkins, and Gilbert Parker were present.

Mrs. S. Sax of Aveleth, Minn., who is stopping at the Schlitz hotel in Milwaukee, was burned by the explosion of an alcohol lamp while engaged in curling her hair.

Ex-Ald. Charles Cooke of Milwaukee was arrested for the alleged acceptance of a $1,000 bribe from the Milwaukee Boiler company in return for a switch track ordinance.

Thirteen coal miners were killed at Bonanza, Ark., by a gas explosion; three miners were killed at Dubois, Pa., by a falling elevator, and a child burned to death at Moline, Ill.

In Chicago Mrs. Robert F. Hale was killed by her husband, who then committed suicide, after confessing responsibility for the death of Miss Margaret Hale from an operation.

The parents of Miss Alice Brewster, Secaucus, N. J., were outwitted by George Martin, who carried on a correspondence with field glasses and a slate. Their marriage resulted.

At Cincinnati three negroes insulted two white women. A riot ensued. John McCarthy, a white man, was stabbed three times and the negroes were saved from death by the police.

As the result of a sensational divorce suit pending in the Lawton, Ok. courts for several months Musey L. Vaughn was shot and fatally wounded by his father-in-law, William Ridley of Durcan, I. T.

Charles and Ophelia Duhme of Cincinnati are charged with recklessness and waste in the management of the estate of the demented young millionaire, Frederick Chase, in an action for an accounting.

"A corps of 400 able, trained workers and a fund of $1,000,000 a year is the goal toward which the anti-saloon league of this country is working," said State Superintendent P. A. Baker of the Ohio league.

CAPTURED. Christian Senf Arrested In California. ACCUSED OF EMBEZZLEMENT. SHORT IN ACCOUNTS HERE WITH THE BIG FOUR. LEFT WITH MULATTO WOMAN. Detectives Say Effie Harris Lived In Richly Furnished Apartments and Wore Diamonds. ALSO HAD A BANK ACCOUNT.
Christian Senf, who was indicted on the charge of embezzling $2,000 or more from the Big Four railroad, was captured in Lathrop, Cal., at 4 o'clock yesterday afternoon. His capture is due to the shrewd efforts of Capt. William Sullivan, Capt. Maher and Detective Ross, who traced him from the time he left Louisville through various cities until he was located. They knew the minutest details of his travels.

Capt. Sullivan declares that he left accompanied by a mulatto woman, Effie Harris, with whom he lived, Capt. Sullivan says, at 1007 West Green street.

Senf was well thought of in Louisville, and has a mother, brother and sister living here at 510 East Madison street. He was cashier at the freight office of the Big Four and Chesapeake and Ohio railroads and was promoted to a higher position Saturday, March 14. His promotion led to the discovery of his series of embezzlements and proved his undoing. Mr. M. L. Akers, superintendent, says that he will employ special counsel and will prosecute Senf to the full extent of the law.

Senf's Course Is Traced.

Capt. Sullivan gives Senf's movements after his promotion as follows:

"Senf knew that another man would take his books when he took his new position, and he knew that discovery of his embezzlement was inevitable. He could not afford to refuse to take the new position, or suspicion would be created. He had been living with Effie Harris for a long time and was infatuated with her. He went to her home as soon as he got off that night, and they took an Illinois Central train to New Orleans. He took a sleeper and she occupied the day coach. The next day was Sunday, and he was not expected to report for duty. He failed to report Monday, but still nothing was thought. When he failed to appear Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday suspicion was aroused and an investigation was made into his books. He was found to be short, but the extent was not known, and the full extent is not yet known. The case was then put into our hands, but he was in San Francisco before we got the case. His apartments at 1007 West Green street, which were occupied by him and Effie Harris, were as handsomely furnished as any in Louisville. She had diamonds and a bank account, and they lived well. Her mother lived with them."

How Detectives Worked.

The capture of Senf was one of the best pieces of detective work ever accomplished in Louisville. The detectives began to work on the case a week after he had left. They found from one source and another that the negress had accompanied him. They got the number of their checks and a description of their two trunks. The New Orleans detectives traced their baggage to Los Angeles. The Louisville department telegraphed to Los Angeles, where it was found that they had gone to San Francisco last Friday. It appears that they heard while at San Francisco that the detectives were pressing them close and they left for Stockton. From Stockton Senf went to Lathrop, a small suburb about nine miles away. Lathrop is also an important railroad center and an ideal place for concealment and easy escape. Meanwhile Elie Harris left San Francisco about Saturday for the East and is now probably near Louisville. The Louisville detectives communicated almost daily with the police at all places where Senf visited and learned of his whereabouts. The arrest was finally made at Lathrop by Constable C. W. Shepard. In a telegram from Constable Shepard last night, Capt. Sullivan learned that Senf is trying to get out of the Lathrop jail on habeas corpus proceedings.

Will Go After Prisoner.

Detective Ross will leave this morning for Frankfort to get requisition papers, and he and Capt. Maher will leave for California to night and bring Senf back to Louisville. Senf was indicted on March 23.

Supt. Akers said last night:

"We have had experts working on Senf's books since he left and the investigation is still in progress. We have found a shortage so far of $2,500 and it will probably exceed that amount. We will prosecute Senf to the full extent of the law."

The charge against Senf in California is being a fugitive from justice. He is twenty-six years old and had a promising railroad career before him. It is said that all his wrong doing is due to the influence of Effe Harris and to his desire to support her higher than his means would allow.

ATTACK ON NEGRO
SETTLEMENT MAY FOLLOW.

Blacks Make Onslaught On Public Hall In An Ohio Town.

Lawrenceburg, Ind., April 9.—A mob of negroes, numbering nearly fifty, armed with various weapons, assaulted the town hall of Cleves, O., this morning, completely demolishing its walls, roof and windows with boulders, clubs and bullets. A number of young white people were dancing in the hall and several were slightly injured. With drawn revolvers the white men chased the black mob away. A running fight through the town following. Many shots were fired. One negro was slightly wounded, but got away. A patrol is

preventing an attack of indignant whites on the negro settlement at Coal City.

GERMS DEADLY AFTER
THIRTY-NINE YEARS.

Young Woman Contracts Smallpox
From Trunk Containing Her
Dead Father's Clothing.

Scipio, Ind., April 9.—Thirty-nine years ago the father of Miss Minnie Peterson died of smallpox. Miss Peterson died of smallpox yesterday, having taken the disease just two weeks after she opened an old trunk containing her father's clothes for the first time since his death.

This is the longest period on record where germs of smallpox have continued deadly. Medical experts have taken great interest in the case. The State Health Board is preparing a scientific statement.

Culmination of a Race War.
Special to the Indianapolis Journal.

LAWRENCEBURG, Ind., April 9.—About 1:30 this morning a party of merrymakers at Cleves, O., six miles from here, were driven from a reputable dance hall by a rain of bowlders upon the sides and roof of the building. Some of the bolder of the young men dashed outside and were met by a scattering volley of stones and bullets. The assailants proved to be a band of nearly fifty negroes. The negroes were pursued by the police for a short distance, but none of them was taken or recognized. Last night's affair is the result of a race war.

Luling citizens form a home oil company with a capital of $25,00 paid in.

Main building of St. Edward's college at Austin burned. It was a dormitory for students.

Counsel leaves Denison to present the liquor case there to the United States supreme court.

Interstate commerce commission asks the Frisco and the Katy to explain their Texas rates.

TROUBLE IN SEAMEN'S UNION
NEGROES ARE THINKING OF BREAKING AWAY FROM IT.
There Are Many of Them in the Organization, but They Say They Get No Jobs Until All the Whites Are Employed Talk of Forming Rival Shipping Office
The Seamen's Union, sometimes accused by the big shippers of having held up as many as ten ships in a single week for lack of men, has some trouble of its own to contend with. Negroes, who make up a good part of the union, have lately shown a disposition to be dissatisfied with the way they have been treated.

For a long time ill feeling between the white and black members has been growing. The negroes assert that they haven't been treated right at the shipping office. In one branch alone, the cooks and stewards' branch of the Seamen's Union, every white member, sixty-seven in all, has found a berth, while not a single negro member was shipped. When members hold up their hands in the union rooms to volunteer to ship on a vessel, the negroes say the whites are invariably chosen.

The fire which has been smouldering in the union broke out in a small blaze on Tuesday afternoon. It came about in a West street branch, where Daniel Allen, a West Indian black, went to claim his shipwreck fee, having been wrecked on the schooner Nellie T. Moore. He spoke English imperfectly and could not make the agent understand his claim, although he showed his union credentials. When he saw that he wouldn't get his money he let out a string of West Indian curses at the agent, who promptly made for him.

According to the negroes, the agent tried to throw Allen downstairs, while several white members of the union joined the agent and rained blows on the negro's head. As a rule, the white members frequent the rooms of the union while the negroes remain in the saloon below. When the negro contingent heard Allen's cries for help, they rushed upstairs to his assistance. As they outnumbered their opponents two to one, the whites scattered.

The whites fled to the street, leaving the negro members in control upstairs. There they formed a ward dance, stamping on the floor and hurling imprecations and challenges to the whites below. They quieted down before the police got there. No arrests were made.

Now the split in the Seamen's Union has appeared. It has long been observed that the negroes in the independent shipping offices have been the boldest and most outspoken against the union, and their brothers in the union are beginning to sympathize with them in their persecution. Broad hints have gone out that the negro element might form a union of its own.

Fields S. Pendleton, a ship owner, with offices at 130 Pearl street, who has in contemplation a Seamen's League, has this to say on the subject:

"There are 1,500 to 2,000 negro seamen along this coast. As a whole, they make good sailors and American vessel owners would prefer to hire their own countrymen, even if black, than employ a foreign element that is always making, or trying to make, a disturbance.

"At present the union discriminates against the blacks by refusing to give them employment, notwithstanding the fact that they are members of the union. The main reason is that the larger part of the agents and walking delegates are made up of the foreign element that cater to the men who come from their own country. Therefore, the American-born negro gets the worst of it."

At the office of the Atlantic Coast Seamen's Union, at 68 Water street, yesterday, no one would say anything on the subject. On the sidewalk were a number of negro sailors who had heard about the outbreak on Tuesday, but each declared that he was not in it. While none of them had anything to say regarding a union of their own, they all agreed that it was almost impossible for them to get a berth while a white man was around who would take the place.

LIVELY FOR A NEW TOWN.
Soperton the Scene of a Warm Shooting Bout. Dublin Ga. Jan 6 Mr. Theo Bog.
Shooting Bout.

Dublin, Ga., Jan. 6.—Mr. Theo. Rogers has returned from Soperton and reports having had quite an exciting time in that new Montgomery county town on the line of the Macon, Dublin and Savannah road. Mr. Rogers states that several negroes endeavored to murder Marshal T. H. Blizzard, firing at him several times. The marshal returned the fire, but no one was hit.

A few nights previous to the attempted murder. Mr. Blizzard whipped a negro named Dave Stokes, who carried a drunken man to his home and put him to bed without the marshal's knowledge or consent. Mr. Rogers assisted in whipping the negro, or was present when it was administered. The friends of Stokes were incensed at the action of Messrs. Blizzard and Rogers, and swore vengeance. A night or two ago they endeavored to put their threats into execution.

On the night of the shooting the negroes came to town fully prepared to murder both of the men. As soon as he learned that his life was in danger, Mr. Rogers started for his boarding house for the purpose of arming himself. He had gone but a short distance before he heard firing. He ran back and found that four negroes had fired upon Marshal Blizzard, but that he was unharmed. The marshal returned the fire, but failed to wound any of the negroes.

None of the negroes were arrested that night, but on the following morning Frank Stokes, Fab Stokes and Bob Brown were arrested. Dave Stokes, one of the negroes wanted, has not yet been arrested, but when Mr. Rogers left Soperton the officers were thought to be close upon his tracks.

After the arrest of Brown, which was effected by Messrs. Theo. Rogers, Charles Outlier and M. C. Dinkins, it was found that he it was who a few months ago endeavored to murder the marshal at Adrian, and for whose arrest a reward of $75 was offered by the people of Adrian. This reward will be claimed by the three men who made the arrest. The three negroes who were arrested, were carried to Mt. Vernon and placed in jail.

FIRED ON BY A NEGRO.
Officer and His Deputy Exchanged Shots With Him. Swainshore Ga Sept. 19—Deputy
Swainsboro, Ga., Sept. 19.—Deputy Sheriff J. E. Thompson had his horse shot yesterday by Bob Brown, a negro, for whom he had a warrant, while trying to make the arrest. Thompson, with another man rode up to the house where the negro was and upon seeing them the negro immediately opened fire from the inside with a 44 calibre pistol. Both men returned the fire, but as the negro was on the inside it is not thought he was hit. Only one shot from the negro's pistol did any damage, striking the horse.

The same negro shot at the marshal of Soperton last year, and it is said he is very desperate. He made his escape, running out at a back door and taking to the swamp.

AT BOYDTON

Anderson Finch Executed and
Doc Eacon Respited.

FINCH MAKES STATEMENT

He Denies His Guilt and Decries He
Knows Nothing of Bacon's Move-
ments that Day—The History
of the Crime.
Anderson Finch Executed and
FINCH MAKES STATEMENT
(Special to The Times-Dispatch.)

(Special to The Times-Dispatch.)

BOYDTON, VA., September 2.—Anderson Finch was hanged here in the jail yard to-day. The drop fell at 12:55. The neck was not broken, but death was produced by strangulation. He was pronounced dead by Dr. Hamilton in fifteen minutes after the drop fell, but the body was allowed to hang for thirty minutes. Finch showed great nerve and ascended the steps leading to the gallows with a firm and steady step. He stated before, and even after, reaching the gallows that he was innocent. His statements have been contradictory from the beginning to the end. He said on the gallows that he was ready to die.

STATEMENT BY FINCH.

The following statement was taken by Sheriff Cogbill by direction of the Governor a few moments before the execution by G. C. Anderson, private stenographer for Sheriff Cogbill:

"Doc Bacon had nothing to do with this that I know of. Nothing at all. I do not know nothing of it, either. I am just as innocent of it as God in heaven. I did not tell the preacher in Petersburg that I did it. I told him that I swore that I did it. My God in heaven knows that I swore a lie when I told it. I do not want to go before my God with a lie in my mouth. I do not know whether Doc Bacon did it or not. I know I did not. I do not know where Doc Bacon was before 12 o'clock. The first time I saw him was on the platform at the depot. If Doc was there I do not know it. I know that if Doc did it I do not know anything about it. I do not know myself what Doc did: I told them that I was guilty to save my own life. My God in heaven knows I was not there. I swore a lie to save my own life. I am innocent and was not there."

FOR DISSECTION.

Finch's body was hipped by express this afternoon to the medical department of the University of Virginia.

The two negroes were brought here yesterday from Petersburg, where they have been in confinement since their trial. They were in charge of Deputy Sheriff Walter Bates and were marched from the depot to the jail and placed in the steel cage. The faces of the men wore expressions of great terror as they appeared to realize that the supreme hour for them was near
A RESPITE FOR BACON.

At 2 o'clock this morning, a telegram was sent to Sheriff Cogbill by the Governor, granting a respite to Dock Bacon, for a short time, in order to allow his case to be heard by the courts on a motion for a new trial.

The sheriff early this morning sent Dock Bacon back to Petersburg. This action of the Governor was based upon Anderson Finch's statement made recently that he had sworn falsely against Bacon, and that he was an innocent man, and that he, Finch, was the guilty man.

During the morning devotional services were held in the jail in which Anderson Finch joined.

THE CRIME.

The crime for which Finch paid the death penalty is fresh in the public mind. One night in the latter part of July Mrs. Charley Geoghagan was left alone (except her little children) at her home. In Chase City, her husband having gone to attend a rehearsal for an entertainment in which he was an actor. About 11 o'clock that night, while Mrs. Geoghagan was sitting alone in her front porch, she was seized from behind by some one and an attempt was made to choke her, and the ruffian at the same time threw meal into her face and eyes, blinding her entirely.

She screamed, and this aroused her children, and their cries frightened the man away.

The next morning Anderson Finch and Dock Bacon were arrested. After their arrest Anderson Finch confessed, saying that he and Dock Bacon together went to Mr. Geoghagan's, and that while Bacon went into the house and attacked the lady, he was watching in an adjoining lot.

There was strong circumstantial evidence in addition to the confession of Anderson Finch, going to show the guilt of Bacon. One was that there was meal found on his clothing the next morning and a knife he had in his pocket had meal upon it. Bacon stoutly denied his guilt from the first.

GOVERNOR WILL INVESTIGATE.

Governor Montague said last night when the confession of Finch was read to him that he would investigate the case further very carefully, and that the negro Doc Bacon whom he respited until Friday, on the recommendation of Commonwealth's Attorney E. C. Goode, of Mecklenburg, would be given perfect justice.

WANT TO LYNCH REPRIEVED NEGRO.
Respited Twice, Virginia Mob Is Afraid He Will Escape Death.
Boydton, Va., Sept. 4.—"Doc" Bacon, a negro under sentence of death for taking part in an assault on a woman, had a close call here today both from the law and a mob. He was to be hanged to-day, after having been respited once. The execution was about to take place, when a telegram came from Governor Montague granting another respite, this time for thirty days.

When the Sheriff with his deputies attempted to take the prisoner out of jail, to carry him back to Petersburg, they were met by a large delegation from Chase City, which had gathered in front of the jail enclosure, and demanded that the prisoner be not removed. The Sheriff summoned a posse within the jail, and for a time it looked as though there would be a clash between the citizens and the posse.

Finally Judge Holmes appeared and addressed the people. He told them that he was satisfied that the verdict of the court would be finally executed and Bacon would be hanged. His words had a quieting effect upon the crowd, which finally dispersed and allowed the prisoner to be taken from the jail. He was put aboard a special train and hurried to Petersburg.

When the Governor's Telegram Arrived.
MOB MADE STRONG DEMONSTRATION
A Conflict Between the Citizens and a Strongly Armed Sheriff's Posse Seemed Imminent When Judge Homes Addressed the Crowd and Pacified Them—Rushed Away.
(Special to The Times-Dispatch.)

(Special to The Times-Dispatch.)

BOYDTON, VA., September 4.—Doo Bacon twice in the very shadow of the gallows is once more afe in the jail at Petersburg. He had a close call here today, both from the law and the mob.

The last religious rites were being said before the march to the gallows, and every detail had been arranged for the execution when the Governor's telegram respiting him for thirty days was handed in. Quite a number of Chase City men were here and considerable excitement existed. The officers had the prisoner in the jail and a strong guard of officers watching over him.

The town authorities as a precaution ordered the dispensary closed as several men in town were drinking.

THE MOB VERSUS THE LAW.

When, the sheriff, with his deputies attempted to take the prisoner out of jail late in the afternoon to carry him back to Petersburg, they were met by a large delegation from Chase City, who had gathered in front of the jail enclosure demanding that the prisoner be not removed.

The sheriff summoned a posse within the jail all heavily armed, and for a time it looked as though there would be a clash between the citizens and the sheriff's posse.

Finally Judge Homes appeared upon the scene and addressed the people from the steps to the jail office. The judge urged the people to desist, telling them that he was satisfied that the order of the court would be finally executed, and Doc Bacon would be hung.

JUDGE QUIETED THEM.

The judge spoke for fifteen or twenty minutes very earnestly, and his words had a quieting effect upon the crowd. They then consented to disperse and allow the prisoner to be taken from the jail.

A special train had been ordered here to hurry the man away, and as soon as he was put aboard, the train moved rapidly away.

Everything is now quiet, and the Chase City delegation has gone home.

Action of the Governor.

Doc Bacon, the Mecklenburg murderer, who was to have been hanged for alleged criminal assault at Boydton yesterday, was given a further respite by Governor Montague and this time for thirty days.

The negro had a very close call and barely escaped being hanged for complicity in the crime for which Anderson Finoh, another negro paid the penalty on the gallows on Wednesday at Boydton.

It will be recalled that upon the urgent appeal of citizens of Petersburg, where the negroes were in jail for safekeeping, based upon an alleged confession of Finch, the Governor granted Bacon a respite of three days, in order that he might look further into the case and see what would develop to throw light upon it, at the hanging of Finch. The latter upon the gallows recanted and instead of exonerating Bacon, he declared him guilty of the crime and pleaded his own innocence.

The Governor then, in order to get at the bottom, and to act intelligently with reference to the matter, sent for Commonwealth's Attorney E. C. Goode, of Mecklenburg, and after a conference with the latter, determined to allow the negro to hang, because upon Mr. Goode's understanding of the case at that time, both he and the Governor believed Bacon to be guilty.

FURTHER DEVELOPMENTS.

It was after this conference with Mr. Goode, who spent several hours with the Governor on Thursday, in which the matter was fully gone over, that His Excellency issued the statement which appeared in yesterday's Times-Dispatch on the subject.

Just before the negro was to hang yesterday the Governor received a telegram from Mr. Goode, in which the Commonwealth's attorney urgently requested His Excellency to grant a further respite of thirty days, as upon further investigation and the learning of some additional facts from the prisoner and other persons, he was clearly of opinion that the negro was innocent.

In discussing the subject last night Governor Montague said: "I have acted throughout this case upon the advice of the Commonwealth's attorney of the county of Mecklenburg and it was upon his belief that the negro was guilty that I issued the statement in yesterday's paper on the subject. Upon Mr. Goode's return home he discovered some additional facts which lead him to believe now that the man is innocent and upon his statement to this effect in a telegram yesterday, urging a further respite of thirty days, it was granted."

SPEECHES COUNSELING MODERATION MADE
Governor Implored to Fully Inform Himself Before Taking Action that Will Make Good Citizens Take Law Into Their Own Hands. Mr. Goode Give Reas- for Asking Respite.
(Special to The Times-Dispatch.)

mass meeting of over 200 representative citizens of Chase City and vicinity was held in the town hall this afternoon. The object was to take some action with regard to the respite of Doc Bacon and allay the excitement prevailing here. Mayor T. D. Jeffress was called to the chair and Professor W. E. Abernathy was chosen secretary. Speeches were made by Judge W. E. Homes, Captain Jeffress and Professor Abernathy.

CONSERVATIVE COUNSEL.

Judge Homes and Captain Jeffress were conservative and urged moderation in expression and no condemnation of the Commonwealth's attorney and Governor Montague, but to believe that they acted from high humane and conscientious motives, and await their explanation for vindication.

Judge Homes and Captain Jeffress were outspoken in opposition to Lynch law and mob rule, while Professor Abernathy was in favor of speedy extermination of any one guilty of assault offense.

THE RESOLUTIONS.

A committee was appointed, who presented the following resolutions, which were unanimously adopted, and the crowd quietly dispersed:

Resolved, First, We want no innocent man's life taken.

Second, We believe with all our hearts that the verdict of the jury and the sentence of the court were just and fully sustained by the evidence, and should now be enforced.

Third, We believe that Doc Bacon is more deserving of death than Finch, who was only accessory to the crime, while Doc Bacon was the prime mover and instigator of the assault.

Fourth, We do not understand why the Governor interfered in the matter without having first consulted with the judge who tried the case, as well as with the prosecuting attorney.

Fifth, We now implore the Governor of Virginia to inform himself fully and act with great care and consideration before he further interferes with the sentence of the law in order that good citizens may not be forced to take the law in their hands to protect our wives and daughters.

Sixth. That a copy of these resolutions be sent to the Governor of Virginia and to the State and county papers.

W. F. CLARK,
B. A. ROBERTS,
H. L. BURWELL,
A. T. FINCH,
LUCIUS GREGORY,
Committee.

Cause of Respite,
(Special to The Times-Dispatch.)
BOYDTON, VA., September 5.—I have just had an interview with Commonwealth's Attorney Goode on the subject of Doc. Bacon's second respite, and he very willingly gave his reasons for making the request of the Governor. Mr. Goode says that he cannot at this time give all his reasons or any reason in full for requesting respite for thirty days for Doc. Bacon, but he states briefly that in view of conflicting statements made by Anderson Finch he regards his evidence as properly stricken from consider- eration of the case; that Finch's evidence eliminated, the Bacon case stands entirely upon circumstantial evidence of such a nature that all the circumstances are required to establish Bacon's guilt; that in the last forty-eight hours he learned through what he considers a thoroughly reliable source that there were witnesses worthy of credence who could and would explain away what he regards as the chief circumstance against Bacon; that he talked with Bacon about this circumstance without giving him any idea of his object, and that he found Bacon's statement very nearly in accord with what the witnesses are said to be ready to testify to; that if these witnesses testify, as he is satisfied they will, Bacon, in his opinion, is entitled to his acquittal, as there would not be more than a suspicion of guilt resting upon him; that, believing this, he felt it his duty to ask the respite thus giving Bacon opportunity to establish his innocence if he can; that if he can do so, no one should want him here; that if he cannot, the law will take its course.

He adds that his is in full sympathy with the people of Chase City, so far as desiring the guilty parties executed, but that of all lynching he regards a judicial one as the worst; that as an officer the responsibility of securing Bacon the respite was upon him, and that he has met it according to his convictions and sense of right.

A gentleman just from Chase City says that excitement is running high there, and that a citizens' meeting would be held there this afternoon.

Judge Holmes was 'phoned for and left here at once for Chase City.

THE GOVERNOR SEEN.

Governor Montague said last night, after he had read the Boydton resolutions, that he could express no opinion regarding them until they came to him officially.

He said, however, that he had acted in the matter according to the wishes of the Commonwealth's attorney, who impressed him as doing his duty in a conscientious manner and without fear or favor. As a matter of fact, the Governor has earn-

THE GOVERNOR ALONE CAN SAVE HIM—THE COMMONWEALTH'S ATTORNEY WORRIED— THE TELEGRAM AND ITS RESULTS.

Petersburg, Va., Sept. 5th, 1903. Mr. John Mitchell, Jr., Dear Sir and Brother: I have just arrived home (Petersburg) from Boydton. Governor Montague gave Doc Bacon three days respite. He did not interfere any further. Anderson Finch was hanged Wednesday evening, Sept. 2nd. Doc Bacon again was brought back to Petersburg for safe-keeping until Friday, Sept. 4th. Deputy Sheriff Beals carried Doc Bacon back to Boydton for execution Friday evening.

BEGGED AND PLEADED.

I only just went to the depot with the intention of bidding Doc Bacon goodbye. He cried and begged so pitifully that I would please stay with him to the last. I decided then that for his comfort, I would go along back to Boydton, as it might make his burden light. Soily way of the S. A. L., we left Petersburg on the 9:58 south-bound train, changing at Lacrosse to the Southern, hence on to Boydton. Three stations before coming to Boydton. Mr. Goode, the prosecuting District Attorney, jumped on the rain.

THE MOB ANGRY.
Night was close at hand. The mole outside was at fever heat. The High Sheriff was busy at work swearing in extra deputies armed with winchester for Doc Bacon's protection. After swearing in, say 25 it was time to make a move, for Boydton was no place to have Doc Bacon after sun-set. Having cheated the ready-waiting gallows when we came to behold, the High Sheriff had already dispatched to officials of the Southern railway company.

They stopped an east bound freight took the engine and caboose and came to Boydton at about a mile a minute. It was now at sun-set. "Respect your county" said he "respect law, order and justice. When these 30 days respite is over the prisoner will be brought back here and be hanged." doc-bacon-boydton-1903-09-04.A20:
CENSURED THE GOVERNOR
The scene here was well described last week in the columns of the PLANET by Rev. J. B. Ferrell. Judge Homes, who presided at the trial was immovable and the resolutions passed by a committee of white citizens censuring the Governor for reprieving Bacon had the matter now stands, many white people regretting the occurrence and express the opinion that an innocent man has been beaten.

A REMARKABLE SCENE.

The scene in the jail here before the execution was distressing. Doc Bacon did not falter, although the light of hope had gone out forever from his eyes. He ascended the gallows with a firm step and showed his abiding faith in the Saviour by declaring that he had nothing against those who had brought about his destruction. He had told the story of his whereabouts and at no time had he wavered in his statement or contradicted himself.

DECLARED HIS INNOCENCE

Standing up before the audience, who were there to see him executed, he declared that there in the presence of the Almighty God in whom he trusted, he had been made the victim of circumstances and was innocent of the crime for which he was to suffer. He hoped that some day that the man would be found who had been guilty of the offense, but that he was not the man. His statement made a most profound impression upon his hearers.

THE FEARFUL PLUNGE.

A moment later, the black cap was adjusted and he had seen the last of earth. A creaking sound followed as the body shot through the trap-door. The body swayed to and fro. There followed a silence, then a convulsive motion and all was over. Doc Bacon had been sacrificed at the behest of a mob. Two lives had been sacrificed for an attempted crime, one of whom was innocent, and the bloodthirsty crowd on the outside retired with the satisfaction of knowing that, whether guilty or innocent, there was one less Negro on this side of the river.

The most distressing part of the affair was the sending of the remains to the Medical Department of the University of Virginia to be used by the doctors for dissecting purposes.

Lynchings in North Carolina.

Raleigh, N. C., August 22.—(Special.)—There have been only two lynchings in this state this year, the last one being in Halifax county. The lynching of a negro was very narrowly prevented this week in Henderson county. PEOPLE OF NEBRASKA ORDER NEGRO TO LEAVE TOWN.
Omaha, Neb., April 21.—Republican Nebraska has no more use for the negro than the democratic south. An organization of business men of a republican town in this state has ordered a respectable negro from the town and has refused to permit him to exist within the town limits.

George Brown, a respectable nergo of Falls City, Neb., several days ago decided to move to Salem, a town in the next county. Brown went to Salem, rented a house and moved his family to his new home. The following evening a mass meeting was held and it was determined, since no nergo had ever lived in Salem, that Brown would not be permitted to remain.

A committee called on the negro and ordered him to leave Salem at once. At first he refused, but later decided to comply and left town today. The arguments used to him cannot be discovered.

Editorial Notes.

A preacher over in Indiana found that he couldn't make a living preaching as his congregation wanted to pay him in pumpkins and old slippers, so he resigned and hired out to John Robinson's circus as a "spieler." Well, if the congregation literally believes religion is free and won't pay, we think it is better to "spiel" for a circus side show than it is to preach for such people. The circus manager will pay.
The Southwestern Editorial Association will meet in Glenwood Friday, April 24th, 1903. As we haven't visited Glenwood since 1872, when we worked on the Glenwood Opinion, guess we will go down and see the boys one day.

Salem, Nebraska, has made a record. A negro came up from Falls City and rented a house and made arrangements to move to Salem. A town meeting was called by the good people of Salem and it was determined that no "nigger" should locate in that town, and the colored gentleman was so informed, consequently he left. If this had been in Louisiana President Roosevelt would have closed up the post office and every 2x4 republican paper in the state of Nebraska would have said it was right. It makes a great difference what state the "poor colored man" is abused in.

Evidence was produced before the Inter State Commerce investigating committee, now in session in New York, examining the hard coal roads combine, showing that the roads charged 250 per cent more for hauling hard coal than they did for any other kind of freight. The government will do its of combining to raise the price of coal, by fining each member of the combination about $300,-000 and five years' imprisonment in the penitentiary at hard labor. If there is any combination that should be wiped off the face of the earth it is the hard coal combination.

Former Postmaster General Smith denounces the Measure.

Harrisburg, Pa., April 22.—Every important newspaper in Pennsylvania was represented at the hearing on the Grady-Salus libel bill by Governor Pennypacker in the hall of the house of representatives. Attorney General Carson sat with the governor throughout the hearing, but neither indicated what would be the governor's action on the measure.

The opening speech was made by Charles Emory Smith of the Philadelphia Press. At the beginning of Mr. Smith's address Governor Pennypacker took exception to his use of the word "insolently" and suggested that it would be well to omit strong adjectives.

Body of a Negro Who Murdered Two Men Found Hanging in a Swamp.

NEW ORLEANS, June 25.—George Kincaid, a negro, who shot John Breck and George Stoakely, was lynched at Cleveland, Miss., yesterday. Kincaid was arrested in Ruleville on Saturday. There were threats of lynching him then, and he was taken to Cleveland for safety. There is some mystery about the lynching, and a disposition to shoulder the blame on the officers of Bolivar county. george-williams-council-bluffs-1903-12-2.A3:
NEGRO SUSPECTS IN JAIL Thought to Be Ones Who Robbed and Assaulted Mrs. Starks and Mrs. Sanders. IDENTIFIED BY ONE OF THE VICTIMS Strong Circumstantial Evidence and Admissions of Their Female Companions Point to Them as Guilty Parties.
In George Williams, alias Burk, and Neely Zimmerman, arrested yesterday afternoon, the police feel confident they have the two negroes who robbed and attempted to criminally assault Mrs. Mary Starks and her daughter, Mrs. Harry Sanders, late Christmas night. In addition to being identified by Mrs. Sanders as the men who assaulted here and her mother, the actions of the two negroes when taken into custody, the police say, indicate their guilt. They were arrested at 1508 Third avenue, where they were found with the two colored women said to have been their companions on the street car Friday night. The women, who gave the names of Emma Eubanks and Della Burk, the latter said to be the wife of George Williams, alias Burk, were also taken into custody. The men were later taken to the county jail for better protection, but the women are being held at the city jail.

The two negroes who assaulted Mrs. Starks and Mrs. Sanders after they left the car at Sixteenth street and Avenue A were accompanied by two colored women who left the car at Fourteenth street, and it was working on this clew that led the police to arrest Williams and Zimmerman.

It was learned that Williams and Zimmerman and the two colored women went to Omaha early Christmas evening to visit friends. Later in the evening the four went to the Colored Walters' club rooms in the basement at Fourteenth and Douglas streets, where they stayed for some time.

Bartender Furnishes Clue.

While waiting for a Council Bluffs car at Twelfth and Douglas streets, the four tried to get drinks at Moran's saloon, but the bartender refused to serve the colored women. The men drank a glass of beer each and then with the women boarded the car. The men took seats opposite Mrs. Starks and Mrs. Sanders, while the women stood up in the alley. The bartender at Moran's saloon has not been over yet to identify the negroes, but the description by him to the police of the two who visited the saloon answers that of the men under arrest. In fact, the description given by the bartender of the two negroes was the first clew which the police say led them to arrest Williams and Zimmerman.

The negroes and their women companions asked for and received transfers to the Fifth avenue line, but when the car reached Sixteenth street on Avenue A, and Mrs. Starks and Mrs. Sanders got off, the two negroes followed, saying to their companions, "Guess we'll get off here," at the same time handing them their transfer slips. The women asked to be let off at Fifteenth street, but the conductor was unable to signal the motorman to stop until the car reached Fourteenth street, when the two colored women alighted. These facts gave the police a direct clew to where the men and women lived.

Seek to Elude Officers.

Detectives Murphy and Harding and Officers Hayes and Lorenzen were detailed to make the arrest yesterday afternoon and they reached the frame cottage at 1508 Third avenue shortly after 1 o'clock. Zimmerman, who answers the description of the big negro who assaulted Mrs. Sanders, was in bed and to the officers he said he had been suffering from rheumatism for two weeks, during which time he had been unable to leave his bed. One of the officers pulled down the bed clothing and Zimmerman was found to be fully dressed except as to his trousers. He was even wearing his coat and vest and it is supposed that when he saw the police nearing the house he attempted to undress and only succeeded in getting his trousers off before they entered.

At first nothing was to be seen of Williams, the smaller of the two negroes, who is said to have been the one who assaulted Mrs. Starks, but a search of the house resulted in finding him curled up in a corner behind a piano.

The men were taken to Twelfth street and Broadway, where the nearest police patrol box is and a call sent for the patrol wagon. By the time the wagon arrived quite a crowd had gathered and had the wagon been delayed any longer it might have gone hard with the negroes under arrest. Hardly had they been placed in the wagon when the crowd made a rush for them and several men attempted to climb in after them. Patrol Driver L. Carlson, however, whipped up his horses and the crowd was soon left behind. There was no demonstration at the city jail and after the men had been searched and booked they were taken to the county jail. Chief Tibbits believing they would be safer there in case there should be any attempt to deal summarily with them.

The patrol wagon then returned to the cottage on Third avenue and the two colored women were taken to the city jail. They are charged with secreting stolen property. The officers, in searching the house, found a quantity of clothing, part of which was identified by William Holder as having been stolen from his yard at 1000 Second avenue as late as Friday night.

Identified by Victim.

The news of the arrest soon spread and by the time the patrol wagon reached the house the second time to convey the women to the jail there were at least 300 men, women and children gathered in front of it. No demonstration, however, was made against the women, although many in the crowd were heard to say that the negroes ought to be lynched.

Before the two negroes were taken from the house Mrs. Sanders was brought there by Detective Murphy and she at once, on seeing Zimmerman, said he was the man who assaulted her. She said that after he had taken her pocketbook the big negro seized her by the throat and told her he intended to commit a worse crime and then

kill her. Mrs. Saunders, also without hesitation, identified Williams as the negro who assaulted her mother. Mrs. Sanders also identified the light colored hat which Zimmerman wore that night and which was found in the house. Mrs. Starks is still confined to her bed from the injuries which she received while struggling with her assailant.

At the city jail Mrs. Eubanks admitted to the officers that she recognized Mrs. Sanders as being one of the white women on the car Friday night.

Zimmerman, it is said, has been working for Contractor Wickham all the summer and Williams had recently been working as a concrete mixer for the Great Western railroad. Both are laborers and both are known to the police.

The police think it possible that the negroes under arrest are the two who attempted to hold up and rob Mrs. P. H. Clark of 1105 Fifth avenue last Tuesday evening on Third avenue, between Eighth and Ninth streets, but were frightened away by the cries of the children accompanying her.

At 9 o'clock last night a number of men began to congregate on Pearl street, in the vicinity of the county jail, and for awhile it looked as if there might be trouble. The crowd, which half an hour later numbered possibly 100 men, was dispersed by the police. Zimmerman and Williams were placed in separate cells on the second tier of the cylinder, and even if a crowd had gotten into the jail the negroes could not have been taken out unless by sawing through the steel bars in front of the cylinder.

REFUSES TO DISPERSE ON MAYOR'S ORDER Dramatic Scene in Court When Prisoners Are Arraigned—Woman Denounces One and Husband Assaulted Him.

About 9 o'clock groups of men were to be seen on the principal downtown streets. Shortly after they began moving toward the county jail. By 10 o'clock several hundred men and boys were gathered in the vicinity of the court house, but it was some time before any attempt to enter the yard in front of the jail was made.

A force of six policemen stood guard in front of the jail for a while and then circled among the crowd urging the members to disperse and go home. Their advice was met with derisive cheers and one of the policemen fired two shots into the air with the evident intent of intimidating the crowd, which by this time had swarmed upon the court house grounds.

Mayor Morgan urged the people to disperse, but the crowd jostled him off the grass onto the sidewalk. About 10:30 some men arrived with a rail from the railroad yards and the crowd began to surge towards the jail. The crowd, however, appeared to lack a leader and no one seemed willing to take the initiative in bringing the rail into play.

"Bring up the rail," was yelled from all parts of the crowd, but no one seemed anxious to comply with the request. In fact, it was plainly evident that the greater part of the crowd consisted of those attracted to the scene out of curiosity and not with any desire to be active participants in a lynching bee.

Makes Break for Jail.

About 1:30 the crowd made a run for the jail and broke down the front door with a stick of timber. Those in the lead surged in through the opening, but here again it was apparent that a determined leader was lacking. The deputy sheriffs on guard were lined up with drawn revolvers and when they commanded the crowd to fall back the order was obeyed and the jail proper was clear of intruders in a few minutes.

At this point Congressman Walter I. Smith appeared on the north steps of the county building and addressed the crowd. He assured the people that the accused would be promptly and fairly tried and if proven guilty punished as befit the crime.

Attorney Emmet Tinley also spoke along the same lines. This, together with the cool determination of the officers in the jail had the desired effect and many left for their homes and the police were able to drive the remainder out of the jail yard into the street.

Nate Bethers and John Knight were arrested on the charge of inciting riot and placed behind the bars in the jail. This had a still further deterrent effect on the crowd, which gradually melted away until only a few remained and no further trouble it is anticipated.

A rumor became current that another crowd, with organized leaders, was forming in the southwest part of the city to make a raid on the jail and as a precautionary measure the Dodge Light Guards were called out to guard the jail, but up to a late hour the crowd had not put in an appearance and it is the general opinion that no further trouble will be experienced.

It was only the lack of a determined leader, however, which prevented a lynching when the jail door was broken down and the disorganized force qualified before the quiet and resolute stand of the deputy sheriffs, who were too few in number to have withstood the rush had the crowd made a determined effort to get at the colored men.

Arraigned in Police Court.

Neely Zimmerman and George Williams, alias Burk, were arraigned in police court yesterday morning. They both denied the charge and their preliminary hearing was charge and their preliminary hearing was continued until next Monday morning.

Williams, who admitted that his right name was Burk, said he was 23 years of age and that he came to Council Bluffs from Macon, Mo., last November and had worked for Contractor Wickham and as porter in a Broadway saloon. Zimmerman said he had worked for Contractors Weaver and Wickham until he had sprained his back about three weeks ago, since which time he had been laid up. Waving his right hand toward the judge he exclaimed dramatically:

"I am innocent of this crime. You can kill us if you want to, but we is innocent, 'fore God, we is."

When Zimmerman made this statement Mrs. Sanders could not restrain herself, and, half rising from her seat, exclaimed: "I'd like to kill you," and her husband made a move forward as if he would like to execute his wife's wish, but checked himself.

Husband Strikes Prisoner.

Sanders was evidently much excited, and when the prisoners were escorted from the court room he made a lunge at Zimmerman and struck him in the face. Zimmerman, although taken by surprise, squared himself off for a fight, but the officers promptly dragged him toward the patrol wagon, while Sanders was forced back by a policeman. The prisoners, who had been brought from the county jail under an escort of seven officers, were returned without further incident, although a considerable crowd was gathered outside at police headquarters.

Sanders was warned by Chief Tibbits against making any further demonstration and he will not be permitted to enter the court room while the prisoners are there until the officers are assured he is not armed, as he made the threat yesterday morning that if he had had a revolver with him he would have shot both of the negroes.

P. J. Moran, owner of the saloon at Twelfth and Douglas streets, Omaha, visited the county jail yesterday and identified the men under arrest as the two negroes who bought a drink at his place Friday night after the bartender had refused to serve the colored women with them and who boarded the car for this city on which Mrs. Starks and Mrs. Sanders were passengers. Mrs. Della Burk, one of the colored women under arrest, who claims to

TWO NEGRO PRISONERS

Mob Shatters Jail Door in

Mayor and Representative Smith Plead
MMINS SENDS MILITIA
Mayor and Representative Smith Plead With Desperate Men and Finally Win the Day.
COUNCIL BLUFFS, Iowa, Dec. 29. For three hours last night a howling mob of men and boys surrounded the county jail, clamoring for the blood of two negro prisoners, and but for the efforts of Representative W. I. Smith and the knowledge that, a company of militia was hurrying to the scene, both men would have paid the penalty of their crime with their lives.

George Williams and Neeley Zimmerman were identified in court yesterday as the men who, after robbing Mrs. Mary Stark and her daughter, Mrs. Sanders, last Friday night, attempted a criminal assault. Both women positively identified the men, and they were held to the grand jury, which convenes next week.
george-williams-council-bluffs-1903-12-2.A9:
MOB BATTERS AT DOORS OF BASTILE COUNCIL BLUFFS NEGROES NEARLY LYNCHED FOR ASSAULT ON TWO WHITE WOMEN. BEGS THEM TO RETIRE Congressman Urges Men to Go Home and Let Law Take Its Course-Militia Not Needed When They Arrive.
BY ASSOCIATED PRESS.

Council Bluffs, Iowa, Dec. 29.—An attempt was made last night to lynch George Williams and Nelly Zimmerman, two colored men, charged with having committed an assault on Mesdames Sanders and Stark last Friday night. The men were in court yesterday, where they were identified by the women, after which they were held to the grand jury, which convenes next week.

Last night a mob of 500 men and boys gathered about the jail where they were confined and demanded that they be turned over by the officers. The demand was refused until midnight, when the mob increased in numbers, until there were at least 1,000 men yelling and battering at the jail doors with clubs. Several times the police charged the mob, but they were unable to break it up.

Militia Not Needed.

Just after midnight, armed with a bar of railroad iron, a dozen men commenced battering at the jail door. A dozen blows shattered it and a cry went up from the crowd.
Congressman Smith, who arrived at this time, managed to secure the attention of George Sanders, husband of one of the women assaulted, and urged him to go home and let the law take its course.

Sanders listened and then started for home. Congressman Smith mounted the courthouse steps and urged the mob to disperse, telling them that Sanders had already gone. This had the desired effect, and inside of half an hour the courthouse grounds were deserted.

The militia had been called out, but the crowd disappeared before they appeared on the scene.

PRISONERS OUT OF DANGER Colored Men Taken to Fort Madison Penitentiary Beyond Reach of the Mob. RUMOR OF SECOND ATTEMPT CAUSES MOVE Done So Quietly that No One Noticed the Prisoners Leave City Jail and Few Caught Sight of Them at the Train.
move the negroes, Neely Zimmerman and George Williams, charged with assaulting Mrs. Mary Starks and her daughter, Mrs. Harry Sanders, to a place of safety. In accordance with this plan the prisoners were taken on the Burlington 5:10 train to the penitentiary at Fort Madison, where they will be kept until the excitement here subsides.

The removal of the prisoners was carried out with the greatest secrecy and not half a dozen persons outside of the attaches of the county attorney's and sheriff's offices knew anything about it until the men were well on their way to the state prison.

Shortly before 5 o'clock yesterday afternoon a hack was driven up to the entrance of the county jail and in it were placed the two negroes, handcuffed together, accompanied by County Attorney, Killpack, Deputy Sheriffs Groneweg and Baker and Assistant County Attorney Hess on the box with the driver. At the depot awaiting the arrival of the hack were Deputy Sheriff Knox, County Treasurer Arnd, Clerk Reed of the district court and several newspaper men. The prisoners remained in the hack, the blinds of which were drawn, until the whistle of the approaching train was heard, and as soon as it drew up at the platform they were quickly hustled through the crowd of passengers into the smoking car. Deputy Sheriff Baker and County Attorney Killpack accompanied them.

So quickly were the negroes hustled into the car that even the passengers on the platform barely noticed them. The only remark heard was that made by one of the passengers in the smoking car, who when he noticed the shackles on the negroes asked the man next him if he thought those were the men they wanted to lynch Monday night.

Prisoners Are Nervous.

Zimmerman and Williams, who had spent a night of terror Monday night, were in a terribly nervous state all yesterday. When Jaller Martin informed them that for their safety it had been decided to take them away from the city they appeared perfectly willing to go, believing that they would be removed under cover of darkness. When they were told the hack was at the door awaiting them Williams, the younger one, almost collapsed, and Zimmerman exclaimed, "Now we will be killed sure."

During the forenoon reports reached the county attorney's office that another and more determined attack was to be made on the jail last night, and after a consultation the removal of the negroes was determined upon. The county authorities have reason to believe that the attack on the jail Monday night was prompted and urged on to a great extent by friends of W. C. Rogers; the prisoner under indictment for the murder of Saloon Keeper Bert Forney last April. "If those fellows break in here the first thing they will do will be to try and kill me, and I should like to have something with which to defend myself."

Needless to say his suggestion that he be given a revolver did not meet with the approval of the deputy sheriffs. Several of the men in the crowd Monday night who were loudest in their demands that the "niggers be taken out and hanged" are known to be friends of Rogers, and evidently thought that it was a good opportunity to attempt his release.

The detail of the Dodge Light Guard consisting of twenty men in command of Captain Van Order, which reached the jail about 1 o'clock, remained on guard until 3 o'clock yesterday morning, when the men returned to the armory and the night passed without further incident.

The arrest of Anthony Wade, a piano tuner, who is almost blind, formed one of the amusing incidents of Monday night. Council Bluffs, Ia., Dec. 29.—Neely Zimmerman and George Burk, the negroes who last night narrowly escaped lynching at the hands of an infuriated mob, were tonight taken to the State penitentiary at Fort Madison, Ia., for safe keeping.

Negro Who Attempted an Assault Upon Mrs. Tuton Tried and Sentenced.

Goldsboro, N. C., Sept. 12.—The negro Henry Holloway, who committed burglary and attempted an assault upon Mrs. Tuton, a most estimable white lady in Greene county some time last month, was convicted in Greene Superior Court at Snow Hill this week and was today sentenced to be hanged on the 16th of October. The crimes for which the negro will hang were committed one afternoon while he was working for the husband of the lady whom he assaulted. Mr. Tuton and the negro were at work curing tobacco some distance from the house. The negro was sent to the house for some tools, and while he was there a rain came up. He slipped into the house without the knowledge of Mrs. Tuton and secreted himself under a bed. When she passed through the room he came out from under the bed and made improper proposals. henry-holloway-1903-08.A11:
HIS NECK SAVED
Henry Holloway Goes to Prison for Life.
Convicted Because of His Voice, There is Room for Doubt of His Guilt and the Governor Commutes His Sentence.
Henry Holloway, the negro who was convicted of burglary in Greene county is not to be hanged, nor at any time.

Yesterday his sentence was commuted to imprisonment for life by Governor Aycock. To urge that he not be hanged Mr. Charles L. Abernathy, of Beaufort, and ex-Judge W. S. O'B. Robinson, of Goldsboro, were here yesterday to present the case to the Governor, who granted executive clemency, this because among other reasons he finds that there is too much uncertainty in the case to take human life.

Holloway was tried at the September term of the Greene county Superior court for the crime of burglary in the first degree, was convicted and sentenced to be hanged. His sentence was respited on October 9th to December 17th, and again on December 17th to December 23d. Today the sentence was commuted to imprisonment in the State's prison at hard labor for life.

The following are the Governor's reasons for the commutation:

"The sentence of death in this case is commuted to imprisonment in the State's prison at hard labor for life. Since the sentence of the prisoner, Hon. Fred Moore the judge who tried the case, has held another term of court in Greene county, and while there carefully investigated the grounds for the application for commutation. He writes me under date of December 17th as follows:

"I respectfully recommend that the sentence of death pronounced upon Henry Holloway at the September term of the Superior Court of Green county be commuted to imprisonment in the State's prison at hard labor for the term of his natural life. After full consideration of this matter and after discussing it with eight members of the jury who tried the case and with many of the best citizens of the county, it is my deliberate judgment that the sentence should be commuted."

"Judge Moore further writes that while he fully believes that the prisoner is guilty there is some room for doubt, and under all circumstances he does not believe the ends of justice demand the execution of the death sentence. The identity of the prisoner as the guilty person was dependent entirely upon the recognition of his voice. A great number of the leading citizens of the county join in an urgent request for the commutation. Six of the jury who tried the case have joined in a written request to me to commute the sentence.

"There is, in my opinion, after a careful examination of the case, too much uncertainty to justify the taking of human life.

"CHARLES B. AYCOCK.

"Governor."
