The subject of education is attracting more attention at this time in South Carolina than at any previous period in the history of the State. The General Assembly has made liberal appropriations for the maintenance of the State colleges and for advancing them to a higher plane of usefulness and efficiency both in general literature and technological teaching, so that there is little excuse for boys or girls to seek institutions of learning outside the limits of the State. Moreover, the denominational colleges of the State are putting forth renewed and commendable efforts to increase the endowment of their respective colleges to keep pace with the advanced ideas along educational lines. And this is a healthful sign of the importance which is attached to education in our state by advanced thinkers and educators of the day. It is an old maxim that "knowledge is power," and in order to obtain that knowledge which gives power, it is necessary that the facilities for the acquisition of that knowledge be afforded to the youth of the country to the extent of the ability of the State to provide them, but not to the exclusion of other meritorious demands upon the liberality of the State. The public school system needs further improvement upon the advance already made over that of a few years ago and we would say that our legislative so'ons have not been disregardful of the right of the masses as to the provision of means, to increase the facilities for the betterment of public school education. It is desirable that the term of country schools be lengthened and the pay of teachers be augmented to correspond with the pay received in many other occupations in life, but it is a deplorable fact that there are large numbers of people in the rural sections of the State who are indifferent to the necessity of giving their children the advantages of a common school education. They need to be educated on this line by talk and persuasion and reading of papers to enable them to understand what their true relation to society, to their offspring is, for we are persuaded that indifference on the part of parents as to their duty to their children arises largely from a want of earnest consideration of the subject. People as a rule are disposed to do right, but they must be made to see it in that light—not by force but by argument. There are other things in this life of more vital importance to society and to humanity than the accumulation of dollars as necessary as that may be in some sense. The development of the mental and moral faculties should be held as of higher value than that of brawn merely. When this idea shall have been engrafted on the public mind then all necessary provision will be made by special taxation to give the country schools equal facilities with the town schools for educating the boys and girls, who after all are the best hope of the future of this country.

soning His Wife

John Black, colored, one of the hands at Haile Gold Mine, was arrested yesterday on the charge of poisoning his wife, who lived on Mr. Lewis Sowell's place in Kershaw county. NEGRO LYNCHED.
Ha Was Charged With Attempted As sault and Identified by Woman Little Rock, Ark., April 7.—John
Ha Was Charged With Attempted Assault and Identified by Woman

Little Rock, Ark., April 7.—John Turner, colored, was lynched at Warren, Ark., Sunday night for an attempted assault on Mrs. W. H. Neeley, a white woman, who resides about seven miles west of town. This attempt occurred last Friday and the negro was arrested Saturday and taken before Mrs. Neeley, who was positive in her identification. Shortly after midnight a mob broke into the county jail, and taking Turner out strung him to a limb in front of the court house, where several other negroes had been lynched at different times in the history of this town. Turner denied his guilt to the last notwithstanding his identification by Mrs. Neeley. There was little noise and parties residing next door failed to hear the disturbance attending the lynching. Not a shot was fired and the body of the negro was left for the coroner, who cut it down and held an inquest, which developed the lynching was at the hands of unknown parties.

joseph-white-newport-1903-08-11.A1:
ROBBED PEOPLE WHO TOOK HIM IN
Cousin of George White Successfully Pursued and a Good Threshing Administered.
Special to the Evening Journal.

Newport, Aug. 12.—This town was thrown into a state of excitement yesterday by the appearance of a colored man being chased by three others, the latter flourishing pistols and guns.

The fugitive was Joseph White, a cousin of George White, who was lynched for his brutal murder of Miss Helen Bishop. He was in New Castle on Monday and that night made his way to State Road, where he stayed over night with a family who did not know him, but took him in and fed him.

When the head of the family arose in the morning he found that White had gone and had taken with him $20, a gold watch, a revolver and a music box. Arousing his neighbors, the man gave chase.

It was learned that a man answering White's description had been seen coming in the direction of Newport. The pursuers followed and found that White had stopped at a house in colored row. The house was approached and the fugitive demanded, but White had jumped the back fence and made tracks across Robert Lynam's field back of the sand hole, across the Snyder farm and into the woods, near the spot where George White had committed his terrible crime. It was here that he was captured by his pursuers after a brief struggle. The money, watch and revolver were recovered, but White had thrown away the music box, finding that it retarded his escape. A heavy thrashing was administered to the culprit and he was released.

A MOB SWINGS TWO
One White, One Black, for the Same Abominable Crime.
(By the Asosciated Press.)

Albany, Ga., Aug. 14.—A white man named Thomas Thompson and King Wrightman, a negro, were lynched yesterday at Hartsfield, in Colquitt county, sixty miles southeast of this place for assaulting Mrs. Mathias, a white woman near Hartsfield last Saturday night.

As soon as the assault was reported a posse was organized. Wrightman, the negro, fled and had been hiding in the swamps. Thompson remained quietly at home, and it is said made no attempt to escape.

The two men went to the woman's home, who is a widow, Saturday night and called her to the door. The negro and Thompson seized her and dragged her out into the yard. Each accused the other as being the principal and the mob, to make sure, hanged both of them.
king-wrightman-hartsfield-1903-08-13.A20:
NEGRO AND WHITE MAN ARE LYNCHED TOGETHER.
NEGRO FLED AND WAS CAPTURED BY POSSE, BUT THE WHITE MAN REMAINED AT HOME.
Mob Took Both Mon Away and Lynched Them Quickly.
Albany, Ga., Aug. 14 — Reports received here this morning are to the effect that a white man named Thompson, and King Wrightman, a negro, were lynched yesterday afternoon at Hartsfield, a little village, in Colquitt county, sixty miles southeast of this place, for assaulting a white woman near Hartsfield last Saturday night.

Full details of the lynching have not been received here yet, but it is known that a posse which had been searching for the negro Wrightman had captured him ten miles south of Albany yesterday afternoon.

Thompson, the white man, it is reported, had not endeavored to escape, and was at his home when the mob captured him.

The two men were lynched to gether by the band of infurated men who had been pursuing Wrightman since the night of his crime.

As soon as the assault upon the white woman was reported a posse was instantly organized, and the hunt for the two men begun.

Wrightman fled and had been in hiding in the different swamps of Dougherty and Colquitt counties.

Thompson had remained quietly at home, and it is said, had made no attempt to escape.

After the mob had secured Wrightman, yesterday afternoon, they went immediately to Thompson's house, where they found him, and taking him with the no-gro, carried him to the outskirts of Hartsfield, and hanged them to a nearby tree.

STORY OF THE CRIME.

On Saturday night, August 1st, Widow Mathis was called to the door of her home, in the little village of Hartsfield, Colquitt county. On opening the door she was seized by two men, dragged into the yard and assaulted. She recognized her assailants to be a white man named Thompson and a negro, King Wrightman. Before parties whom her cries attracted arrived the assailants had fled.

Thompson went to his home, not thinking that he would be molested, and the negro took to the swamps.

Thursday morning information as to his whereabouts was received and a posse of seven men started out in pursuit of him. He was caught in Dougherty county, ten miles below Albany, and carried back to Hartsfield.

On the way back to Hartsfield with the negro the posse called by Thompson's house.

He, too, was taken in charge by the men.

Late in the afternoon they reached the little village where the crime occurred; and there Thompson and his negro confederate were strung to the same tree.

It could not be learned by the men just what part each performed in the crime.

The actual assault being charged to the other by each. So the posse lynched both the negro and the white man.

SENTENCED TO PRISON. Was Guilty of Cruelty Toward Hundreds of Soldiers. Berlin, Aug. 20.—Sergeant Breidenbach, of the Eleventh infantry, has been sentenced to three and a half years imprisonment for mistreatment of private soldiers. There were 1,500 mild and 300 serious offenses charged against Breidenbach. He so severely whipped a recruit recently as to cause the man to commit suicide. DETAILS BRITISH FORCE OF 30 WHITES AND 500 NATIVES Attack Town of Burmi and Kill 700 Home Defenders.
Home Defenders.
London, Aug. 20.—Dispatches received at the Colonial offices today from Zunguru, Northern Nigeria, dated August 17, give details of the destruction of the town of Burmi by a British force of thirty whites and 500 native rank and file. The enemy's loss was seven hundred killed, including the former Sultan of Dokolo and a majority of the chiefs. The British loss was eleven men killed, including one officer and 62 men wounded. The enemy made a desperate house-to-house resistance.

GAVE RISE TO RUMOR.

Cardinal Rampolla Will Not Be Secretary.

Rome, Aug. 20.—Pius X having several times received Cardinal Rampollo in long audiences, the rumor obtained currency that the cardinal might be reappointed secretary of state to the Vatican. A denial, however, of this rumor has been obtained from a reliable source. It is expected that the conferences were due partly to the desire of the pope to become personally acquainted with all foreign questions, and partly to the fact that Cardinal Rampolla, being the executor of Pope Leo's will, must consult with the pontiff whenever controversial points arise.

Mgr. Kennedy, rector of the American college, gave a dinner tonight in the villa of the American college at Castel Gandolfo, in honor of Most Rev. J. J. Harty, archbishop of Manila. Among the guests were Cardinal Satolli, Mgr. O'Connell, rector of the Catholic university of Washington, and Mgr. Fowler.

BOWEN TALKS OUT.

Will Go Wherever He Is Sent, Even to North Pole.

Berlin, Aug. 20.—The Lokal Anzeigent today publishes an interview with Herbert Bowen, U. S. minister to Venezuela in which Mr. Bowen is reported to say that he does not regard it as peculiar that he should represent two countries before the Hague tribunal.

"Neither does my government," he said. "I go where I am sent, even to the north pole. I take the part only of the weak against the strong. I cannot understand the attacks of the German press on Baron Von Sternberg. I learned to know him as a clever diplomatist and a nexcellent upholder of German interests.

"It almost seems, Mr. Bowen is reported to have said, "that the friendship that America feels for Baron Von Sternberg is regarded in Germany as a sin."

HANGED BY A MOB.

One Negro Confessed and Another Is Under Arrest.

Halifax, N. C., Aug. 20.—A negro who confessed to having assaulted and murdered Mary Jenkins, a 13-year-old white girl, was tonight hanged by a mob to a tree and his body riddled with bullets. The negro confessed after the noose had been placed around his neck. After disposing of the negro the mob, which made no attempt at concealment, dispersed. The body of the child was found in the stable of Captain Griffith, her grandfather, tonight with her throat cut from ear to ear. A negro employed by Captain Griffith when searched was found to have the keys of the stable, a bloody knife and blood on his hands and clothes, and he was at once arrested by citizens.

STEAMER SPRUNG A LEAK.

Crew and Two Young Ladies Were Rescued.

Cleveland, Aug. 12. The ore steamer Queen of the West, bound from Cleveland to Erie, sprang a leak and sank a few miles off Fairport, Ohio, today. The crew of fifteen men and two daughters of the engineer were rescued by the steamer Codorous. They had a narrow escape from drowning. One seaman was seriously injured.

SHIP NOT ADMITTED.

Bubonic Plague Appeared at Valparaiso After Vessel Sailed.

Guayaquil, Ecuador, Aug. 20.—The Chilean steamer Napocho, from Panama, bringing the American and European mails, passengers and cargo, arrived today but was not admitted, because when northward bound she left Valparaiso after the appearance of bubonic plague there. manna-ponton-halifax-1903-08-20.A18:
THE HALIFAX HORROR

The Negro's Fiendish Work With Rope and Knife.

His Victim Was a Delicate Child Just Recovering From a Spell of Sickness.
(Special to News and Observer.)

Weldon, N. C., Aug. 21.—Manna Ponton, the negro who brutally outraged Miss Mary Jenkins, the twelve-year-old grand-daughter of the late Captain J. M. Grizzard, at Halifax, last evening, was swung up to a telegraph pole early this morning and his body was riddled with bullets. Ponton confessed the crime, which for brutality was the darkest ever before known in Halifax county.

The little girl went out about 6 o'clock to look for a hen's nest. She failed to return when search was made, her little body was found in the stable tied up in a bag. She had been choked to death with a piece of rope and afterwards the negro cut her throat with a case knife. The negro at first denied all knowledge of the crime. When asked why blood was upon his hands he said he got it cleaning fish. Later he confessed that he caught the child at the stable, outraged and murdered her.

Seventy-five people went down from here, and people poured into Halifax from all sections. The officers of the law made a faint effort to protect their prisoner, but the body of determined men who surrounded the prisoner took him quietly into hand and with hardly a word spoken they made quick work of it. Even the negroes are dumb in the presence of such a crime, and not a few say Ponton deserved instant death.

The grief of the child's mother is something terrible, and while friends and neighbors stand by with tears of sympathy, no human being can lift the dark veil of night that has fallen upon the home. Little Mary Jenkins was a fair-haired, delicate child, never at any time strong and just up from a spell of sickness.
manna-ponton-halifax-1903-08-20.A29:
BLACKEST CRIME OF THE AGE.
Foul Murder in Hautaf.
It is not an uncommon thing to read of murders, assaults and outrages away from home, but the people of Halifax county now realize what such things mean.

On Thursday evening August 20th, at her home in Halifax, little Miss Mary Jenkins, the grand-daughter of the late Capt J. M. Grizzard, was missed by her mother upon returning home from a call down the street. Search was made for the child who was a delicate girl of twelve years, and her body was found in a stable not a hundred feet from the back door steps of her home, assaulted and foully murdered. She had been caught, a cord drawn around her neck to strangulation and then her throat cut. To heighten the horror of the affair the mother found her own child in this condition with the little body still warm after the assault, suffering and death. The body was found in a stable, but soon it was discovered that the deed had been committed in a feed room near by and a knife was found in the feed room with fresh blood. The stable in which the body was found was locked and the keys were in the pocket of a young colored man named Manna Ponton. He was at once suspected of the crime and was promptly arrested. He denied it and when blood was found on his chinna nail he told various tales about it. Said he had cleaned fish; but when his sister with whom he lived said they had not had any fish the negro said he sold them to a man in the country after he had cleaned them.

When the knife was produced he confessed the crime. Said he was in waiting for the little girl who was accustomed to go about the stable. He told her there were eggs in the feed room, and when she went in after the eggs he seized her and choked her and tied the cord around her neck; and afterwards cut her throat.

As soon as he made the confession there was no more chance for his life. One might as well have stood on the sea-shore and said to the in-rolling waves, "Aback! Come not further!"

The little girl was found about 7 o'clock and before midnight Manna Ponton's body was hanging to a telegraph pole not far from the depot with hundreds of bullet holes which riddled him from the crown of his head to the soles of his feet. His body hung there until 2 o'clock the following day when it was taken down, carried to the county home and buried. Hundreds of persons were present when the wretch was killed and hundreds came in from the country next day to look upon his body.

On Friday afternoon the body of the murdered little girl was taken to the Methodist church where services were held by the Rev. Mr. Cotten. It was perhaps the saddest funeral ever held in the historic old town of Halifax, for it was the result of the blackest crime ever recorded in the annals of the State.

Raleigh Post.
Under the caption of *Anarchy and Its Provocation* we find the following in the Washington Post. It needs neither addition, embellishment nor comment. The tale of horror which calls for the Post's comment is founded on fact both in statement of a particular crime and for the earnest appeal.

The letter of "A Southern Woman" and the observations and inquiry of the Post thereon disclose a condition all too palpable. The criminal in the case recited was promptly denounced, and his prompt execution as firmly approved by reputable colored men of the same community, and we insist these reflected in their expressions the sincere sentiments of a large element of the colored people of that and other communities in this State. Such occurrence will meet with just such prompt reprisal on part of the white people; the only trouble to be averted is that all good citizens of both races must insist that the punishment be confined to the guilty and not permit what too many evidences indicate is a growing disposition, a brutal condemnation of or assault upon every member to which the guilty wretch or wretches belong. For God sake let the soberminded men of the State and the country insist on discriminating between those who behave and those who commit crime. To the latter let very, very swift justice be done by a punishment that fits the crime.

But here is the article from our Washington contemporary which needs to be read by all men, black as well as white, North as well as South:

"A Southern woman writes and the New York Herald prints, one of the saddest and most harrowing stories it has ever been our misfortune to read. It is the story of the outrage and foul murder of an innocent and beautiful little girl, just twelve years old. This frightful tragedy occurred in a North Carolina town, although the Herald withholds the names and places at the suggestion of the writer. The object of the letter is not vengeance. The 'Southern Woman' merely makes a plea for more lenient judgment of those who take vengeance into their own hands.

"We quote a brief extract from the narrative:

"Will you listen to a true story? It is horrible, so horrible that not even the gifted Harriet Beecher Stowe could have described its heartrending misery. It happened yesterday. The defiled, mutilated body of the little white girl is still unburied. Come with me and I will show you the very spot where the horror took place, not two hundred yards from the court house, a stone's throw of the child's home.

"See enter this stable a beautiful blue-eyed, flaxen-haired maid of 12 years, the only daughter of a widowed mother—her joy, her pride, her darling. The child had been sent by her mother to get some eggs that she knows are in a nest there. A black man sees her go in, and follows her. If the child knows he is behind her she doubtless feels no alarm. He is the hostler; she has known him all her life, sees him every day around the barn.

"When he reappears he locks the door. His hands and clothes are bloody, and he steals stealthily away.

"Soon the mother, wondering that her daughter does not return, goes to the stable to look for her, finds the door locked. Possessed with the awful uneasiness that seizes every white mother of the South when her girls are long out of her sight, she calls to a little boy passing by, helps him to climb to the window. He calls the child's name, but there is no reply. Peering about, he sees a bag in a corner. There is blood running from it. Soon a crowd from the village is there. The lock is broken, they enter the stable, the bag is opened, the murdered child is before them.

"That she was choked into insensibility to prevent an outcry is evident, for her pretty blue eyes have started from their sockets. To be sure that she will never be able to tell who has so defiled her the fiend has cut her throat from ear to ear."

"The Herald is furnished with all needful references for the ascertainment of the facts. Presumably, the Herald made sure of them before it published a story so indescribably hideous.

"It is hardly necessary to say that the fiend was captured. The case was not one in which a mistake could possibly be made. They identified him beyond doubt—by the key of the stable, by the blood of his victim, and, finally, by his own confession. They hanged him within six hours of the crime. No man in the community or its neighborhood felt that he could breathe freely while that unutterable demon lived. And the writer of the letter adds—for this is the real object of her appeal:

"Once more, I beg, try to be sorry for the white women of the South. All are in danger; from the four-year-old babe to the grand-mother of sixty-five.

"Aye, and pity the white men, too, that are frenzied by such crimes. Reason with them like brothers.
manna-ponton-halifax-1903-08-20.A39:
OUTRAGE CONDEMNED.
Leading Negroes of Halifax Denounce Crime of the Negro Rapist Ponton.
One serious mistake the negroes make is in denouncing lynching, with never a word of denunciation or warning against the crime which causes lynching. Sympathy is usually with the victim of the lynchers, rarely with the victim of the lynched. Now and then there is a rare exception and here is one of them. In a communication to the Raleigh Post signed by M. W. Williams, (Rev.) A. J. Jackson and John H. Collins, as committee, for whom the Weldon News vouches as among the best negroes of Halifax, these sentiments are expressed:

"We, the colored citizens of Halifax, N. C., do condemn the murder and outrage committed on the 20th day of August upon a white child 12 years of age in our historic town by the negro and human brute Manna Ponton. We do hereby pledge ourselves to use every means within our reach to stop the heinous crime of rape that is so common within the confines of our State. We ask the ministers of the Gospel, school teachers and all good citizens to resolve themselves into a committee of the whole to prevent said crime by using the best means suited to the occasion. We do not encourage lynching and would prefer the law to take its course, but circumstances very often alter cases. The said Manna Ponton was hanged and shot a few hours after he committed the damnable crime. The right man was caught and made a confession. The fate that he met for his crime was not too severe, and we hope that it will be a warning to all evil-doers, and deter them from committing atrocious crimes.

"The better class of colored citizens in our town will not countenance crimes, and will do their best to stop outrages and bring the offender to trial at all hazards."

WITH BLOODHOUNDS NEGRO IS CHASED IN TEXAS.
If He Is Caught, He Will Probably Be Lynched.
Be Lynched.

New Braunfels, Tex., June 30.—Armed men are to-night pursuing with bloodhounds a negro man who to-day attempted to assault, and mortally wounded Mrs. Emil Gronle, wife of a farmer who lives five miles southeast of this point.

The negro appeared at the Gronle home and demanded money. Before the woman could reply, he seized her and threw her to the floor. The negro was armed with a razor, with which he slashed his victim across the abdomen.

Bloodhounds were secured from San Antonio and put on the trail of the negro. Mrs. Gronle is still alive, but is not expected to survive the night.

There is every reason to believe that the negro will be lynched if caught.

CRUM APPROVES LYNCHINGS.
Charleston's Colored Collector Takes Unexpected Ground on Mob Law. Collector W. D. Crum, of Charleston, S. C., has shocked his fellow negroes by advocating lynching. At a meeting in Chicago Tuesday night he said: "Lynchings savor of the barbarism of the dark ages, but we must think of the crimes that provoke them. These crimes are so atrocious that no punishment is too severe for them. "Lynchings is not a race problem," said Dr. Crum. "There is no north or south, but the form of unlawful punishment is general all over the country. The most horrible lynching which ever took place in this country occurred in Delaware only a few days ago. Such punishments savor of the barbarisms of the dark ages, but we must consider the crimes that provoke them. They are so atrocious that no punishment is too severe.

"Too many persons denounce lynchings without considering their cause. If the law was quick and decisive there would be fewer lynchings. "The remedy is to exterminate the horrible wretches that commit the crimes—not by killing them, but by teaching them better."

CUT ALMOST IN TWAIN.

Crime of Horrible Atrocity Reported
From New Braunfels, Texas.

A special from New Braunfels, Tex., says: Many posses of armed men are pursuing with bloodhounds a negro man who attempted to assault and mortally wounded Mrs. Emil Grofile, wife of a farmer who lives five miles from town.

The negro appeared at the Gronle home and demanded money. Before the woman could reply he seized her and threw her to the floor and with a razor slashed his victim across the abdomen, almost severing her body. The dogs about the yard set up a barking and frightened the negro away.

NEGRO DENIES HIS GUILT The Supposed Murderer of Mrs. Annie Gronle in Jail in San Antonio. Capture Was Made in Caldwell County and He Was Brought to San Antonio Under Military Escort With a Mob of Frenzied Men at His Heels Eager for His Life.
that the negro charged with the murder of Mrs. Gronle is on the south bound I. & G. N. train and will reach San Antonio after 12 o'clock." This was the substance of a long distance telephone message from New Braunfels shortly before 12 o'clock yesterday, which was received by a well known citizen. Word was passed around and the news traveled like wild fire that the real murderer of Mrs. Gronle was en route to San Antonio. The information, however, was too late and when the train pulled into the depot there were only fifteen citizens and officers present. Glistening bayonets could be seen in every window of the first coach of the train. As the train came to a full stop the New Braunfels militia company in command of Captain Guinn, of that place, took positions just outside and pushed the crowd back that was fast assembling on the scene. A few minutes later the prisoner attired in a blue mother hubbard and white sun bonnett made his appearance surrounded by officers. The troops were again ordered to fall in and they escorted the officers and negro to carriages and then disbanded and returned to their homes on the 12:30 north bound train. In the meantime the alleged slayer of Mrs. Gronle was taken to the county jail for safe keeping. According to the statement of one of the troopers who accompanied the negro to San Antonio, the accused man had a narrow escape from lynching at New Braunfels. When it became known that Mat Kimble, the negro, was in jail, a great crowd numbering some 500 people assembled and demanded the negro. The sheriff cautioned the crowd against any acts of violence and pleaded with them to leave the law take its course.

"Had the train been a half hour late I doubt whether the negro would be alive at this moment," exclaimed the soldier, "as we only had five minutes notice to turn out and it was a case of fight our way from the jail to the train with our prisoner."

Arriving at the local county jail Kimble was made to change his clothes, after which he was brought into the north room in front of the jail where the officers of Bexar, Comal and Guadalupe counties plied the prisoner with questions concerning the killing of Mrs. Gronle. To all questions leading up to the killing of Mrs. Gronle, Kimble stoutly asserted his innocence. He gave out a statement to the officers giving his whereabouts previous to the murder and after and people whom he was with up to the time of his arrest. Sheriff Tobin duly warned Kimble beforehand that whatever statement he made would be used against him in the future. To this Kimble assented and said that he could neither read or write. The accused is a coal black negro, apparently about 25 years of age and appears to be somewhat ignorant in a great many ways, but his answers to the officers yesterday were intelligent. When apprehended Kimble wore two pair of trousers, one of which was a pair of white check goods answering the description given by the murdered woman. The other pair was of a dark blue, common make and was splashed with mud and contained several red stains which will be submitted to a chemist today. His shirt was of a heavy light colored stuff and was in tatters. The shoes worn were on the brogan order and they were ready to fall to pieces.

The negro was captured by Lum Stokes, a deputy sheriff of Guadalupe county, and Mat Hutchen, a constable from Kingsbury, who followed a supposed trail over a winding course of sixty miles, the chase lasting from Wednesday, the day after the crime, until Saturday morning. He was taken to Seguin and placed in jail, but although he maintained his innocence the prevalence of mob sentiment induced the officers to steal the prisoner out Saturday night and carry him in a hack across the country to New Braunfels, where they arrived at 3 o'clock Sunday morning.

The officers after locking Kimble up in a cell resorted to a little strategy to obtain a confession from the accused. For this purpose they secured a negro detective named Sandy Williams in the same cell and the prisoner was made to believe that Williams was placed there as an accomplice. On being alone in the cell, Wililams said to Kimble confidentially:

"I outraged a white woman once. But I told this high-sheriff all about it, and he got me out of it. You tell Mr. Tobin the truth and he'll get you out of anything."

Sandy stayed with Kimble from 12 o'clock until about 3 p. m., when Kimble told him that he wanted to send for the sheriff and make a confession.

Sheriff Tobin and Constable Stevens responded and went to the negro's cell. A confession was then made, but on account of leading questions which had been asked, and the method used to

get it, the officers were not satisfied and about 5:30 o'clock went back to the jail and had the negro repeat his statement circumstantially in his own way. He told the purported story of the crime from beginning to end, and his account was clear and convincing. Both statements were practically the same, the story being drawn out by persistent questioning.

Kimble made a statement going into the details of the crime. He said that he had demanded money from Mrs. Gronle and stabbed her with a pocket knife. This pocket knife he said he threw into the weeds, and ran away. His statement covered revolting details, all of which were recanted by him when questioned by the officers last night.

Sheriff Tobin later gave out a statement that he would protect the prisoner and the sheriff a half hour later received a message from Governor Lanham, which read as follows:

"John Tobin, Sheriff, San Antonio, Tex.: Hold Comal county prisoner charged with rape until further orders from me. "S. W. T. LANHAM, "Governor."

At 9 o'clock last night Kimble sent for Sheriff Tobin and Constable Stevens and said his previous confessions were untrue and were made on the hopes held out to him by Sandy Williams, the negro who was locked up with him.

There was some talk of lynching Kimble yesterday and crowds of people congregated in front of the jail, but those who gathered there were satisfied to speculate on the outcome and no attempt was made to resort to violence. It is said that several necktie parties were organized between San Antonio and New Braunfels, but that they were too late in reaching the stations and catching the train on which Kimble was a prisoner.

The following interesting account of the capture of Kimble by Deputy Sheriff Stokes is given:

The trail was first taken on Wednesday, the next day after the assault. It was in Mr. Sipp's pasture, four or five miles east of where the tragedy occurred. Mr. Sipps told Stokes that a man answering to the description of the wanted negro had passed through his pasture the day before. He thought the negro was after a horse, and halloed at him, when he ran in the direction of the Guadalupe river.

About twelve miles east of Seguin the trail was struck again on Thursday. Here Mr. Stokes was informed by a boy that he had seen a negro in a near-by field and had called to him, thinking he was a party who was to meet him there. But the negro had run. This field was near Kingsbury, and Constable Hutchen joined the pursuit here.

The fugitive was trailed by the tracks of his bare feet through fields and pastures to his home. He skillfully eluded all houses and roads and traveled altogether about sixty miles.

Early Saturday morning near Fentress, about two and a half miles from his home, the pursuers came upon a house occupied by negroes and situated in a field. As they rode up, a man dashed off into a patch of high cane. Stokes rode in after him and he surrendered. The negro was Mat Kimble.

STORY OF THE CAPTURE.
Mob on Negro's Heels and State Troops Called Out for Protection. Special to The Daily Light.

New Braunfels, Tex., July 6.—A negro who is believed to be the one who murdered Mrs. Annie Gronle last Tuesday near New Braunfels was captured by Deputy Sheriff Stokes, of Guadalupe county, near Fentress, Caldwell county, Saturday morning.

Sheriffs Stokes and Nowotny brought their prisoner to New Braunfels yesterday morning at 3 o'clock. It was soon rumored over town that the negro had been captured, but some said he was in the jail at Seguin, others said he was in the San Antonio jail, and some believed that he was in jail here. People began to congregate around town and soon gathered near the jail. This correspondent sought an interview with Sheriff Stokes and was told positively that the right negro had been captured and taken to the jail in San Antonio. Sheriff Nowotny took the prisoner to the jail here in a roundabout way, but the people were suspicious and gathered around the jail door and were there when the prisoner was brought

out. The officers tried to disguise him by putting a woman's dress and bonnet on the prisoner, but the dress was too short and his trousers showed beneath the dress. Sheriff Stokes, with the negro, started for the station with a large crowd of people following.

A few cries of "Mob him!" "Burn him," were heard, but there was no one to lead and no organization. They reached the I. & G. N. depot, where the officers locked the prisoner in. There were several hundred people crowded around the depot, and some of them seemed determined to keep the officer from taking him away to San Antonio, but the determined look on Sheriff Stokes' face and his hand on his trusty gun deterred anyone from making any attempt to take the prisoner from him. The people asked the officers to let the prisoner stay in the jail here till he was better identified and they would promise not to hurt him, but the officers refused to do so.

Sheriff Nowotny called on Captain M. E. Guinn to order out the military company to aid in protecting the negro from the mob and Captain Guinn soon had his company in line before the door of the I. & G. N. waiting room. When the train drew up to the station, the negro was hurried into the coach with the officers and soldiers all around him. The people here were cool and collected and there was little talking done. The negro, dressed in woman's clothes, with his trousers showing beneath the dress and his bonnet over his face, presented a comical appearance.

He answers to the description given by Mrs. Gronle before her death. Sheriff Stokes said that he trailed this negro during the past five days from Zipp's pasture, near the scene of the crime, to near Fentress, about forty miles away. He tracked him eight miles through fields and pastures and finally came upon him hiding in a cane patch. The negro was barefooted and had on two pairs of pants when caught. He seems to be about 20 years old and is very black.

The negro denies committing the crime, but Sheriff Stokes feels sure that he has the right man. He trailed him from near the scene of the tragedy, and the negro went through fields and pastures and kept away from the road and was hiding out when caught.

Before the train left, Captain Guinn telephoned Austin to get authority from the governor or adjutant general as to whether he should take the military company out of the county or not to accompany the prisoner to San Antonio or Seguin. It is believed here that if the prisoner is taken to Seguin he will be mobbed.

The military company which took the negro to San Antonio returned to New Braunfels after having turned the prisoner over to Sheriff Tobin. Just after the train left here for San Antonio the adjutant general wired Captain Guinn to take charge of the prisoner and protect him. Fifteen minutes later the adjutant wired him:

"Never mind previous orders, as I hear that the prisoner was taken from the train at Bracken and mobbed." This was a false report, however, as the train did not stop in Bracken, and the negro was safely turned over to Sheriff Tobin at the I. & G. N. station in San Antonio and quickly lodged in jail there.

Miguel Escobedo and his wife of Cholulu, Mex., fought a duel which resulted in the death of both parties. After a bitter quarrel the couple decided to fight a duel without seconds or witnesses. Armed with revolvers, the husband and wife took positions in a room in their home and fired simultaneously. The woman was shot through the head and died instantly. The man was shot through the head and mortally wounded. He lived long enough to tell about the duel, but refused to divulge the cause of the trouble.

R. M. Love, comptroller of the state of Texas, was assassinated in his office at the state capitol in Austin by W. G. Hill, a former clerk. Hill entered Love's office, and, while conversing pleasantly, suddenly pulled a revolver and fired two bullets into his body, death resulting instantly. Hill searted to leave the office, when a clerk grappled with him. In the scuffle Hill's revolver was discharged, the bullet fatally wounding the assassin. Hill had been a clerk is the comptroller's office for several years, but was dismissed when Love took charge. It is believed the man had brooded over his discharge until his mind became deranged.

A dispatch from Lexington, Ky., says that Gen. Cassius M. Clay and his former child-wife, Dora Richardson, will be reunited, living under the same roof, at least, if not remarried. When the girl, then in her fourteenth year, was married to Gen. Clay she had been courted by Riley Brock, a neighborhood boy, who was running barefoot about the little village of Valley View, and she could not forget him. When her childhood sweetheart signified his wish to make her his wife she became indifferent to her aged husband, and told him she wanted her young sweetheart. The Sage of Whitehall did not wish to give up his young wife, but when she cried and begged, he consented to divorce her. Brock had joined the army, and, returning, and, in the eyes of his sweetheart, although she was the wife of the former minister to Russia, the famous abolitionist and duelist, he was a hero. Gen. Clay gave her a home in Woodford county and furnished it for her, even to having hung on her walls the costly bric-a-brac and beautiful paintings he had secured while in the land of the czar, as the representative of the United States. Brock soon tired of the place, and sold out everything. Gen. Clay sought to get the girl to come back to him, and she did go back to Whitehall, but took her husband with her. Gen. Clay ran him off with a shotgun, and soon the girl followed. Brock was killed a few days ago by a railroad train at Longview, Ill., and upon learning of his death Gen. Mr. J. C. Burt, the gentleman referred to in Monday's Light as the officer who started out to hunt up evidence as to the whereabouts of the negro Mat Kimble, before, during and after the alleged crime of the murder of Mrs. Gronle, near New Braunfels just one week ago yesterday, returned this morning from his long self imposed task in the interest of justice. Mr. Burt is not an officer but a volunteer, to satisfy himself alone. Having known Kimbel and his people he journeyed over the ground on horseback, step by step, visited every place and saw every man and boy in field or cabin named by Kimble, took sworn affidavits to every bit of testimony as to Kimble's whereabouts on that day and returning this morning presented to Sheriff Tobin and Chief Deputy Captain Nevill an array of sworn facts proving conclusively that the negro was 25 miles distant from the scene of the commission of the crime at precisely the hour alleged. COUNTY COURTHOUSE NEWS THE MAT KIMBLE HABEAS COH PUS CASE. The Negro Who Was Accused of the Awful Murder of Mrs. Gronle, Near New Braunfels, Was Heard Today on Application for Bail.
The Thirty-seventh District court room, in the county courthouse, was the scene of all interest to some three counties this morning—Bexar, Guadalupe and Comal—when the habeas corpus application of the young negro, Mat Kimble, came up for hearing at 10 o'clock before Judge Clark. Kimble is accused of the criminal assault upon and murder of Mrs. Gronle, a young married woman, who lived on a farm four miles west of New Braunfels, in Guadalupe county, for some years, and up to the Friday following the commission of the awful crime, which occurred on Tuesday morning, June 10, of the present year. Kimble was arrested by Deputy Sheriff Stokes, of Guadalupe, near Kingsbury, where he had formerly worked. He has been in the Bexar county all since.
since.

At the hearing this morning there were fifty-seven witnesses sworn and put under the rule. These are from the three counties named. Hon. Carlos Bee represented the prosecution and Attorneys John Goodrich and Theo Gibbs, of Seguin, are representing the defendant. In the examination of seventeen witnesses this morning, little, very little, new light was thrown upon the already known particulars of the crime, and none of the witnesses could positively identify the prisoner as the negro whom they had seen in and near New Braunfels and near the Gronle place on the day of the assault.

The defendant was released from the charge and ordered held until further orders of the court at the request of his counsel.

A RACE WAR.

THREE FOUND DEAD AND SEVEN OR EIGHT WOUNDED WHEN SMOKE BLOWS AWAY.
CONSTABLE TURNED BACK BY NEGRO WITH SHOTGUN
Official Gathers Posse and While on Way to Serve Warrant Is Fired Upon From Woods and a Pitched Battle Ensues.
BY ASSOCIATED PRESS.

New Orleans, Oct. 20.—In an encounter between a band of negroes led by a white man and a constable's posse, three negroes were killed and seven or eight wounded near Pecan Grove plantation in St. Charles parish. None of the posse was hurt. The surviving negroes and their white leader, Pat McGee, fled to the swamps and are being searched for. Further trouble is feared.

McGee and the negroes have been working for the Mississippi Valley railroad. Recently complaint has been made that some of them had contracted debts and refused to pay. Charges were filed and a constable went out to see the negroes.

On his way he met John Hinds, a negro assistant of McGee, who covered him with a shotgun and commanded him to keep away from the camp.

The constable returned to town and organized a posse. Near the camp the posse encountered 18 of the negroes and McGee, all heavily armed. Both sides concealed themselves in the high weeds and a battle of 20 minutes followed.

The negroes and McGee finally lost their nerve and fled.

The bodies of three dead negroes and several others wounded were picked up when the smoke cleared away.
pat-migee-1903-10-20.A13:
THREE NEGROES KILLED.
Seven Also Wounded in a White Posse's Charge on a Railroad Camp.
NEW ORLEANS, La., Oct. 20.—Three negroes were killed and seven wounded seriously in an encounter with a Sheriff's posse at Pecan Grove Plantation, in St. Charles Parish, about thirty miles above New Orleans, yesterday. The negroes were railroad hands working on the Yazoo and Mississippi Valley Railroad, which is raising its tracks. They were eighteen in number and were under the command of a white man named Pat McGee.

Constable Charles Sorgy attempted to serve a legal notice on one of the negroes Saturday, but was driven from the camp by a negro. He summoned five other white men and the entire party, well armed and on horseback, accompanied him to the camp. As the posse approached McGee and the negroes fired on them. The shooting was kept up for some time, the negroes finally scattering and taking to the woods. Three negroes were found dead in the fields and seven wounded, who were cared for in the neighboring settlement, Elkinsville. None of the whites was wounded.
pat-migee-1903-10-20.A24:
ANOTHER BUTCHERY.
REPORTS tell of a butchery of colored men in the rear of Pecan Grove Plantation, St. Charles Parish, Louisiana, October 19th, 1903. Three colored men were killed and eight wounded. These colored men had been working for the Mississippi Valley Railroad and are alleged to have refused to pay certain bills said to be held against them. White men organized under the leadership of a constable and proceeded to kill them as above stated. The newspapers call it a race war instead of a race butchery, as only colored men were killed.

This condition of affairs will continue as long as colored men submit to it. In conflicts with the lower strata of white men of these localities a colored man has nothing to expect but death and he should resolve to sell his life as dearly as possible. His maxim should be to "kill and be killed." There is no other way out. It should be remembered that, according to the Christian's belief, "death is the gate to endless joy."

Of course, no one likes to go through it by the "shot-gun route." Still its all the same at last and colored men should see to it that they have company. There are numbers of good white people in the southland, but there are millions of the other kind. Politeness to white and colored people, manhood and a determination to sell our lives as dearly as possible when we are called to go are the elements which will simplify the situation and bring respect to those whom we have left behind.

William B. Jolliffe, of Millwood, died on Sunday, aged 66 years. Labor is so scarce in middle Virginia
William B. Jolliffe, of Millwood, died on Sunday, aged 66 years.

Labor is so scarce in middle Virginia that farmers are helping one another to save their crops.

Oliver Fields, colored, is in jail at Williamsburg on a charge of attempting to assault Mrs. C. E Masters.

Mrs. Eliza Taylor, widow of W. H. Taylor, died at Winchester Saturday night, aged seventy-four years.

A race riot is threatened near Blue Ridge Springs because a number of white men whipped a negro woman for insulting Dr. Early's wife.

The Central Labor Union has decided to organize the negro workmen at the Newport News shipyard. It is understood some negroes will fight the movement.

A marriage that elicited much surprise and interest and among the members of the Virginia colony in Baltimore took place yesterday. The parties were Hugh Caperton and Mrs. Mattie Booth Kyle.

Miss Rebecca Latham died at the Winchester Memorial Hospital yesterday from consumption. She was a daughter of the late Thomas M. Latham, of Winchester, and was seventy-four years of age.

A cablegram states that the Chesapeake and Ohio steamship Shenandoah arrived at Liverpool safely from Newport News. It was reported last week that the Shenandoah had been lost at sea.

The contract for the construction of a drydock at the navy yard at Norfolk yesterday was awarded by the Navy Department to John C. Rogers, of New York, whose bid of $910,000 was the lowest.

The monitor Arkansas arrived at the Norfolk navy yard yesterday. She kicked her turret loose by trying to fire her 12-inch guns simultaneously. The turret will have to be removed and the guns taken out, as in the case of the monitor Nevada, now at the yard.

Anderson Finch and Dock Bacon, the negroes charged with attempted criminal assault on Mrs. C. E. Geoghegan at or near Chase City, who were take to the jail of Petersburg Saturday evening for safekeeping, were yesterday taken to Boydton under strong guard for trial.

George Washington Griggs, the negro who attempted to criminally assault Marion Mason, the four-year-old daughter of Mr. J. B. Mason, of Port Norfolk, was tried yesterday before Judge Portlock, and found guilty. He was sentenced to 18 years in the penitentiary.

Both Fowler and Dikes were unarmed, although Hicks claimed he was fired upon by them first. Hicks was arrested and placed in jail.

Ten thousand dollars in notes is due the Shenandoah Valley National Bank, $4,000 to the Union Bank and the rest to other creditors. PHILADELPHIA, July 27.—The British tank steamer Baku Standard arrived today with a hole in its bow as a result of a collision with an iceberg. The vessel was steaming slowly over the Grand Banks of Newfoundland during a dense fog on Monday morning when an iceberg about 200 feet high loomed up dead ahead.

The engines were reversed, but before the steamer could be diverted from its course, it struck the submerged portion of the iceberg. A small hole was stove in one of the forward compartments below the water line. The pumps were placed in operation and by this means the water was kept down.

rosa-kaiser-manchester-1903-06.A1:
POSSES OUT WITH DOGS
THEY SEEK A SUPPOSED NEGRO MURDERER AND RAVISHER.
Old Man Assaulted Near Lawrenceburg and His Daughter Presumably Outraged and then Killed.
Special to the Indianapolis Journal. LAWRENCEURG
Special to the Indianapolis Journal.

LAWRENCEBURG, Ind., May 22.—Posses with bloodhounds to-night are scouring the country around Manchester for a negro, who waylaid and assaulted Martin Kaiser and his daughter Rose, aged seventeen years, near Manchester, last night.

Kaiser was found near the Big Four tracks early this morning in an unconscious condition. After regaining consciousness he said that a negro had assaulted him with a club and carried his daughter into the woods near by. The girl's hat and umbrella were found near Tanner's creek today, and it is believed her body was thrown into the creek by the negro after he had assaulted and murdered her. Kaiser, who is seventy-three years of age, is in a critical condition to-night and is not expected to live.

Kaiser and his daughter had been to the Catholic Church at Yorkville to attend Ascension day services. They passed through Manchester soon after 7 o'clock last evening and the attack must have taken place soon after. A colored man seen near Manchester yesterday afternoon is suspected. Excitement is at fever heat tonight and if the guilty man is apprehended he will probably be lynched.

Kaiser describes the negro as being tall, slender, very black, wearing a small black moustache, black suit, black shirt with laced front, and with a black soft hat slouched well over his face. He says the negro was armed with a broken pickhandle. Word was received here late to-night that a negro suspect was arrested at Cleves, O., twelve miles east of here. He was lodged in jail awaiting the arrival of the Manchester authorities.
rosa-kaiser-manchester-1903-06.A10:
DRIVING OUT THE NEGROES.
Murder of Anna Kaiser Leads to General Threats Against Them.
Murder of Anna Kaiser Leads to General Threats Against Them.

INDIANAPOLIS, May 24.—Excitement over the murder of Miss Anna Kaiser, and the brutality that accompanied it, is unabated in Dearborn and adjoining counties and the people are taking revenge upon the negroes and are ordering all of them to leave the county under penalty of death if they are found there at the end of three days. Two contractors who are employing large gangs of negroes on the grade for an electric line were notified to-day to discharge the negroes and not to employ any more on the work.

Seven negro families that lived near Manchester station, where the tragedy occurred, were driven from their homes last night, and it was with difficulty that the conservative citizens stopped the mob from burning their homes.

There is no doubt but Miss Kaiser was murdered by a negro, and in the present state of excitement the disposition is strong to hold the entire negro population of the county responsible for the crime.

Some of the negro families who were driven from their homes have taken refuge in Lawrenceburg and will be protected.

An autopsy was held to-day on the body of Miss Kaiser. The negro assailant of the young woman carried her to a dismantled church, a quarter of a mile from the scene of the attack upon the father. The girl made heroic resistance. Hardly a bone in the girl's body was whole and her face was battered almost beyond recognition. The autopsy showed that the girl resisted him to the moment of death.
rosa-kaiser-manchester-1903-06.A12:
NEGRO SUSPECT IS FREED
NO EVIDENCE OF HIS COMPLICITY IN ROSA KAISER'S MURDER.
Stoned and Cursed by a Mob as He Leaves Lawrenceburg—Reward for Murderers of Sutton and Yeager.
pecial to the Indianapolis Journal.
LAWRENCEBURG, Ind., May 25.—Louis Everson, alias Black Ponto, the negro held here for identification as the murderer of Rosa Kaiser, was escorted down the Big Four tracks beyond the city limits this evening by Sheriff Axby and Officers Petcher and Justis and told to make himself scarce, an order which he lost no time in obeying. He was followed for fully a mile by a hooting mob of men and boys, who cursed, stoned and beat him. He finally escaped, and was last seen entering a strip of woodland, where he is supposed to have sought concealment.

Although no incriminating evidence could be secured against Everson, there are many persons who still believe him to be guilty, and it is probable that he will be sought out and tarred and feathered, if no worse fate is meted out to him, unless he makes good use of his liberty.

The release of Black Ponto was occasioned by the receipt of a telephone message from the mayor of Rising Sun to the effect that the warrant issued for him in that city several months ago, had been withdrawn. The mayor added that the further Everson remained from Ohio county the better it would be for his safety, as he probably would be mobbed should he venture to return there so intense is the feeling against him.

The search for the negro suspect seen in Seymour on Friday night proved fruitless, as did the search for the negro who tried to assault the Schmidt children at Weisburg yesterday. The search for alleged white accomplices has been abandoned.

A petition requesting the contractors in charge of the Big Four improvements between Lawrenceburg Junction and Sunman's to dispense with colored labor, is being circulated by Louis Kaiser, brother of the murdered girl. The presence of so many negroes is regarded as a menace to the community and unless the contractors heed the request embodied in the petition it is believed that a war of extermination will be inaugurated against the blacks by the incensed friends of the murdered girl.

Physicians in attendance on Mr. and Mrs. Kaiser report that the aged couple are improving slowly, but are not yet out of danger.
rosa-kaiser-manchester-1903-06.A14:
FARMERS ARE AGITATED.
Threaten to Lynch Suspected Negro Murderer.
Threaten to Lynch Suspected Negro Murderer.

Lawrenceburg, Ind., May 26.—Sunday was a day of intense excitement in this county over the murder of Rosa Kalser and the murderous assault of her father last Friday. The farmers gathered here, at Guilford, at Manchester and other towns in this county and openly threatened lynching if the guilty person could be identified. Sheriff Axby has a strong guard of deputies at the jail where Louis Everson, known as "Black Posto," is held on suspicion. There is no doubt but that this negro would have been lynched but for the announcement that Albert Harding, who came here from Manchester, did not identify him as the negro who had called at the home of Mrs. Mary Griffin shortly before the assault on the Kaisers, and none of the other neighbors could identify the prisoner.

While the crowds were coming into town a dispatch was received that another outrage had occurred in the county, and this diverted them from the jail. Sheriff Axby and deputies were called in the morning to Weisburg, where an unknown man supposed to belong to some railroad construction crew was said to have assaulted the two little daughters of George Smith, a farmer. The sheriff was joined in this chase by many farmers and also by Rev. M. F. Cowdry and his bloodhounds.

The negro has not yet been found and farmers are still scoring the country for him.
rosa-kaiser-manchester-1903-06.A15:
Negroes Ordered to Leave.
Negroes Ordered to Leave.
Indianapolis, Ind., May 27.—Farmers in Dearborn and adjoining counties are making a determined war upon negroes as a result of the murder of Miss Anna Kaiser. Many familities have been ordered to leave, and negroes employed by farmers are being discharged. It is estimated that 100 negroes have been driven out of the rural districts of the county in the last three days. Yesterday a committee of farmers, headed by a brother of the murdered girl, waited upon the superintendent of the Big Four Construction Works at Guilford, and notified him that the negroes employed by him must leave.
rosa-kaiser-manchester-1903-06.A25:
Weekly Constitution's "Big Three"
Bill Arp.
I AM Jesus Christ, the carpenter's son. My mission is to save sinners. I fought in the civil war from Dalton to Jonesboro. Twice I have been president of these United States since the surrender and have attended all the reunions up to date, but now they have got me penned up here as a Tennessee lunatic and won't let me go to New Orleans. I can't get a passport because I am Jesus Christ. Can't you do something for me? I want to go and rejoice with those who rejoice and weep with those who weep."

That poor fellow has my sympathy. Maybe if they had let him go with the veterans it would have restored his reason. I know it brightened up our boys and now they can't talk about anything else. Was there ever such glowing, growing patritoism? It looks like the number increases at every reunion and that without pensions. The Grand Army of the Republic has reunions, but it is mainly to keep up the pension grab, the thing that Tom Benton called "the bottomless gulf of charities and gratuities."

I saw it stated the other day that 70 per cent of the federal army were foreigners or foreign-born and were fighting only for those rebels down south, and I move we quit trying. We've been working on 'em for nearly forty years and have never converted one yet." As they marched through New Orleans 100,600 strong you could hear that same old rebel yell from St. Charles to Vicksburg. Old Father Mountcastle told me it bursted every telegraph wire south of Mason and Dixon's line and away up in Pennsylvania the Western Union had to cut down their poles for a hundred miles.

But I'm distressed about Mississippi. Who is Governor Longino, anyhow? His name is not in any biography that I've got. I reckon it wasent worth putting in. I reckon he is a foreigner or he wouldnt have invited Roosevelt, the slanderer, down to Jackson to help lay the corner stone of the capitol. Roosevelt said that Jeff Davis was the arch repudiator and while governor vetoed the bill that made provision to pay the repudiated debt, and he has never retracted nor apologized for that lie. I wonder if Longino knows that Governor McNut was the author of repudiation and gave as his reason that the money was borrowed from Baron Rothschild, in whose veins flowed the blood of Judas and Shylock, and whose mortgages would confiscate our cotton fields and make serfs of our children. That's what he said in his message, but the legislature wouldnt vote for it, and it took five years to get the bill through. All this time Mr. Davis was fighting for his country in Mexico and got desperately wounded at Buena Vista and had to use crutches for six years. He never was in the legislature nor was he ever governor, and yet Roosevelt, the slanderer, lets the lie stand and Longino invites him down to lay the corner stone. Oh, my country! When will all this tadychom and hypocrisy cease? Oh, Mississippi! How are the mighty fallen!

Now these utterances are my own—neither the editor nor any paper is responsible for them. My feelings and emotions are all my own. I honor the memory of Mr. Davis and have profound respect for his widow, and there is no limit to my contempt for the brute who put manacles on him or the conceited historical who slandered him. It is a comfort to dispense them both.

And now, three cheers for Indiana, the champion state for lynching negroes when they commit outrages on their women. Not a week passes but there is a fresh case and the people turn out and scour the country for the brute. And now they are driving all the negroes out of a county where an outrage was committed. You see they have no chain gang there and but few negroes. Lynching has almost stopped in Georgia because punishment is more speedy, and there is a chain gang in sight in almost every county, but let a sure-enough case come up and a sure-enough lynching will swiftly follow. There are more than 7,000 men in our state who have not bowed the knee to Baal—and the Rev. Newell Dwight Hillis shouldn't sleep in a bed in my house unless he was sick unto death.

But enough of all this. It sounds like I am mad with somebody, but I am not. We are all happy at my house tonight, for our far-away boy is on his way home. We have just had a telegram from him and he will be here tonight. He lives in Mexico City and it has been three long years since we have seen him. This is Carl, the youngest boy—the pet of his mother—the one she loves the best and prays the longest for every night. He will stay with us a few days and then go away again and perhaps never see us any more. My wife has been saving the spring chickens for him and the flowers are not to be cut till he comes, and the strawberries are still bearing and the cake is in the oven. Nothing is too precious for Carl and he and Jessee will sing their old songs and rehearse their happy days when we lived in the country on the farm.

Oh, the happy, happy days on the farm, before our boys all left us and our girls got married!

But we are happy still and love everybody, except some—

BILL ARP.

COUGER TO MOVE QUARTERS.

A Law of Life.
And now the marshal investigating the horrible murder of the Kaiser girl near Lawrenceburg declares that it was impossible for the unknown negro that was suspected of the crime to commit it; the alibi is complete in his case. What becomes now of the negro lynching bee and race war, discharge of all negroes at work in the vicinity, the driving out of all negroes from Dearborn county, and so forth and so on? Moreover, the theory is now entertained that revenge by some enemy of the Kaisers was the motive of the crime, and that the criminal was a white man. The episode should be emphasized in the hope that it may leave its lesson, which is the old one of insistence on law and not passion to deal with crime, and above all, of refusing to act as though people of a certain color of skin were predisposed to crime. The spirit of revenge manifest here, the spirit that tolerates whitecappism and makes it possible, the spirit that makes lynching possible—which is the same that tolerated the talk in this case—is the spirit of of barbarism. It may never be indulged in lightly. There is no royal road to progress. The price of advancement, of civilization as well of liberty, of eternal vigilance. Nat' s as well as men are liable to fall y from grace. rosa-kaiser-manchester-1903-06.A30:
THE NORTH'S NEGRO PROBLEM
SOUTHERN VIEW OF CERTAIN RECENT OCCURRENCES.
Indiana Way of Avenging Crimes Against White Women-The Same Matter in Ohio-Conditions in the South That Cause People to Resort to Lynch Law.
White Women—The Same Matter in Ohio—Conditions in the South That Cause People to Resort to Lynch Law.

MACON, Ga., June 6.—The agitation of the negro question in the North is watched with much interest and not wholly without amusement by the people in the Southern States.

Of course, such demonstrations of wholesale hatred of negroes in general and threats of something like a war of negro extermination as have come to the front recently in Dearborn county, Ind., are greatly deplored by all respectable people in the South. To be sure, Southern people, unfortunately, are in a position to appreciate the fury provoked necessarily by the unspeakable negro crime which aroused the citizens of Indiana to such blind rage. Yet, even with all due allowance for that wrath, it is contrary to Southern practice and Southern principles to visit upon an entire negro community the punishment due to one individual.

Chasing away all the negroes of a neighborhood, as has been threatened in the Indiana county mentioned, just because one particular negro committed a shocking crime, is not regarded here as in any way defensible. It is looked upon as another of the frequent manifestations of utter intolerance of the negro which invariably breaks out in communities of Northern people, whether they be in the North or the South, whenever the negro problem in any of its worst aspects is suddenly brought home to them.

Out of the New South there has grown the new negro, and with the new negro has come a new negro crime—the crime against white women which with a certain type of negroes has become a sort of obsession and which before the days of reconstruction, to say nothing of the days before the civil war, was unknown in the Southern States. A Northern clergyman a few weeks ago denied that that crime exists among the negroes of the South.

"I wish," said a Northern man, who is a Republican, who served in the Union Army all through the war and who now lives in Louisiana, "I wish," said he, "that that Northern preacher would come down here with his family and live for a winter, he would change his mind.

"I lived for a time in the country. The post office was two miles away. When I went to get my mail I almost invariably took my wife with me, and when by any chance I could not, I closed every window and shutter in my house, locked and bolted her in the upper rooms and locked and bolted every door.

"Even then I never came back to my house without fear and trembling. I would not again go through such months of dread as I went through then for all the wealth of the country."

"I live five miles out in the country," said Hooper Alexander, one of the leaders of the Atlanta bar, "and within a short distance of my home two white girls, mere babies, have been murdered by negro ravishers. There is a grove a little way back of my house and I would no more let my little child enter it alone than I would let her enter a jungle filled with tigers."

In view of the record in this form of crime made by the new negro in the South, it is not to be wondered at that Southern people, many of whom have been driven to abandon their country homes by sheer dread of these roving wild beasts, are indignant when such a man as the Northern clergyman in question, speaking out of the fulness of his ignorance, makes the assertion that the crime referred to does not exist among the negroes of the South.

That it does exist, that it is one of the disheartening facts which those who feel most kindly toward the negro have to encounter, is a proposition which no man, unless one whose ignorance of the subject was strongly involved and intricate, would ever for a moment think of disputing.

As long as negroes perpetrate this crime just so long will negroes by lynched. They are lynched for it in Ohio and other Northern States where the excuse of an overwhelming, semi-barbarous negro population does not exist. In certain parts of the South where white people live at wide distances apart and where they are surrounded on all sides by a dense negro population, conditions have come to a pass, with the evolution of the new negro, which, in a way, are analogous to frontier conditions where stray settlers were surrounded by Indians.

Methods in both cases are resorted to which are beyond the pale of the orderly proceedings of the law. While those conditions exist and while the negroes persist in that particular crime which rouses men to a blind fury of wrath, and until there is a radical change in the whole composition of human nature, lynchings, so far as man can see are inevitable and beyond repression.

So the people of the South are in a position to understand the feelings of the citizens of Indiana. They can understand and condone the headlong wrath which moved them to hunt for the negro who committed the characteristic negro crime—to hunt for him for the purpose of hanging him whenever and wherever he chanced to be caught.

In the same way Southern men are able to understand why crowds of influential citizens of the vicinity of St. Clairsville, Ohio, a few days ago tried to find and lynch two negroes who attacked a white woman there. Yet, with all that, the spirit which leads the Indianans to wreak their vengeance upon an entire negro population is greatly deplored.

This is a form of negro agitation in the North that is regretted here. Already negroes in the South are suffering from this same sweeping Northern intolerance wherever in Southern States there are enough residents from the North to have weight in the community.

As for some of the other forms which the negro agitation in the North is taking—the debate, for instance, precipitated recently by the Rev. Dr. Parkhurst, as to whether the proper designation of a colored person is "nigger" or "negro"; the ambition expressed a few days ago by another well-known preacher to officiate as chambermaid-in-waiting to a distinguished Ethiopian—all these and similar ramifications of the debate are affording a little innocent amusement in connection with a subject which, for Southern people, unhappily is, in its general aspects, only too grave and sombre.

MURDER OF ROSA KAISER
DEARBORN COUNTY SHERIFF HOPE- FUL OF CLEARING UP CRIME.
Lawrenceburg Marshal Indulges in Some Sherlock Holmes Deductions— History of the Black Deed.
Special to the Indianapolis Journal.
LAWRENCEBURG, Ind., Sept. 2.—Sheriff John Axby returned here to-day from Cincinnati, where, in conjunction with the police of that city, he has been making strenuous efforts to locate a young man named Otto Pool, who is wanted by the Dearborn county authorities on a grand larceny charge and who, it is believed, can clear up the heretofore impenetrable mystery surrounding the murder of pretty Rosa Kaiser, which occurred near Manchester station last May. At the time of the murder Pool was employed on the Big Four Railway improvements in progress between Manchester station and Guilford, Ind., and on the day preceding the crime he, in company with three suspicious-looking characters, were seen hanging about the Kaiser home. However, suspicion did not point to him until recently, when the police learned certain facts, which they do not care to disclose at present.

Sheriff Axby claims to have in his possession evidence implicating Pool in the murder of Rosa Kaiser, and believes that if the young man is arrested he will be glad to secure leniency by divulging all he knows about the case.

Detective Crawford, of Cincinnati, holds a warrant for Pool's arrest on the grand larceny charg
The murder of Rosa Kaiser is the darkest crime that ever blackened the criminal annal of Dearborn county. Late one evening in May, when the girl, in company with her aged father, Martin Kaiser, was returning home on foot from Yorkville Catholic Church, where the father and daughter had been attending Ascension day services, she was murdered in cold blood and her body thrown into West Fork, a branch of Tanner's creek, where it was found horribly mutilated a few days later. Martin Kaiser was attacked and felled to the earth unconscious by a blow from a heavy club dealt from behind, a gaping gash was made in his throat and he was beaten brutally. The assailant then threw him into the creek, where he revived hours afterward and made his way home more dead than alive. Kaiser did not witness the assault on his daughter, as she was many yards ahead of him, running to escape a heavy storm that was approaching. From this fact it would appear that the man was struck down first and the girl, seeing the attack on him rushed to his rescue and met her death. Her umbrella, which was broken about five inches from the tip, indicated that she had made a fierce struggle in defense of either her father or herself. Martin Kaiser did not see the assailant. The blow which rendered him unconscious was struck from behind, and he could give no details other than that he heard a footfall behind him, received the blow and all was blank. Some deductions in the case which have never been made public were the result of a personal investigation of the crime on the part of Marshal Theodore Crusse.

"When Kaiser was struck he was facing the west," said Mr. Crusse to a Journal representative this morning. "He carried an umbrella raised to keep off the rain
the west, said Mr. Crusse to a Journal representative this morning. "He carried an umbrella raised to keep off the rain which had just begun to fall. The storm was coming from the east, and therefore the umbrella was slanted in that direction. The blow which felled Kaiser was received upon the left side of his face and was dealt from behind. Such a blow must necessarily have been delivered by a lefthanded man. When the police capture a lefthanded suspect, I will share their belief in his possible guilt."

Heretofore all efforts to locate the murderer have proved futile. Shortly after the discovery of the crime the country for many miles about Manchester station was scoured by armed posses searching for the guilty one. They were aided by blood-hounds, but even the keen-scented manhunting dogs were at fault. Now it is hoped that the mystery will be at last cleared up, and the girl's murder avenged. Martin Kaiser, who has fully recovered from the effects of the assault, is heartbroken over the loss of his wife who died recently from the effects of the shock of her daughter's horrible death.

Three Negroes Have Close Call From Mountaineers.
Nashville, Tenn., August 10.—By a narrow margin a triple lynching was averted in Winchester, Tenn., this afternoon. The intended victims were Henry Judge, Joe Delp and John Evans, and tonight, after a close call, they have found security in the Davidson county jail here, where they were brought by Sheriff Jim Stewart of Franklin county.

The men are charged with the murder, near Winchester, of aged Simon Booker and his wife and the cremating of the latter's remains in the Booker home, which was set on fire by the murderers. The crime was committed on Tuesday last and feeling among the mountaineers of that section has steadily grown.

Friday the last of the suspects was arrested and when this became known, preparations for a lynching began. Today a well-organized mob of four hundred men came into town and proceeded to the jail. The sheriff had been appraised of their approach and hurriedly left with his prisoners, reaching the railway station by a circuitous route. By the time the mob discovered their absence they were well on the way to Nashville.
