simon-booker-winchester-1903-08-05.A13:
MURDER WILL OUT.
JOE DELP CONFESSES TO THE CRIME OF KILLING
Old Man Simon Booker and His Aged Wife, and Burning their Home.— Implicates Others.—Says They were Paid to do It.
Winchester, Tenn., Aug. 18 — Joe Delp, John Evans and Harry Judge, the three men charged with killing old man Simon Booker and his aged wife, burning their home and cremating their bodies, according to the confession of Delp are all guilty. For fear of mob violence here, they were taken to Nashville last week, but now that the excitement has partially subsided they have been returned here.

When the men were placed in jail in Nashville they were confined in seperate cells. This was done for several reasons. It was deemed precautionary by Sheriff Cartwright in order to prevent the men from plotting or even conversing. It was thought, too, that they would the more readily take someone into their confidence and tell of their crime if allowed to remain alone.

Delp all along has manifested more of a disposition to talk than either Judge or Evans. He was in a cell in the lower cage and was the only one of the trio on the first floor. Evans and Judge being upstairs in different cells. All of the men were guarded at first in their speech, but the confidence of Delp was finally won and he made the following confession:

"Judge is the man who hired me and Evans to do the work. He and old man Booker had some trouble about a lumber deal, and he was sore on the old man. He wanted to get him out of the way. Then, too, there were others around there, but I am not calling any names, who had it in for old man Booker. They were to put up a part of the money which Judge was to give. We were to get over $100. Judge was to pay $10 of the amount. It was said that old man Booker had told the revenue officers about moonshining end other violations of the Internal Revenue laws, and several of his neighbors had it in for him.

"We agreed to do the work for Judge. He hid a shotgun in a little out house near Simon Booker's place. He told us where it was, and Evans and I went down there one evening. We went into the house and Evans told the old man he wanted to see his garden. They went out in the garden. Evans taking the gun. Evans said he wanted to see the potato patch and they went over there. When they got there Evans stepped back of the old man in a potato row and shot him in the back.

"Then he came into the house and shot Booker's wife and set the house afire. I never had anything to do with the shooting or the burning of the house, but I went along and saw it all. I will make this confession in court when the trial comes up."

Judge vigorously denies that he had anything to do with the killing. He says he don't know anything about it. Evans is rather reticent on the subject, but states that the others are as guilty as he is.

The three men are now in jail in Winchester, and it is believed there will be no further danger of mob violence. The Circuit Court of Franklin County convenes this week, and it is believed the men will get a speedy trial.

Sentenced to Hang.
Joe Delp and John Evans, the convicted assassins of old man Booker and his wife, were sentenced to be hanged October 9. Judge McReynolds told the defendants that they were convicted out of their own mouths, and that it would have been a prostitution of justice had the jury returned any other verdict after listening to their confessions.

After pronouncing sentence Judge McReynolds asked the defendants if they had any statement to make. Delp, in a low but distinct voice, said that he had told the whole truth. Evans declared dogmatically that he was not guilty, and sat down.

THREE MURDERERS MEET
DEATH ON THE GALLOWS
Slayers of the Bucher Family Are Executed at Winchester, Tenn.
HANGING AT PITTSBURG
WINCHESTER, Tenn., May 5.—Henry Judge, Joe Delp and John Evans were hanged here to-day for the murder of Simon Bucher and his wife last August. The trap was sprung at 5:43 a. m. The three men exhibited the same indifference and stolidity that marked their conduct during the trials, and walked without assistance on to the scaffold. Each of them made a short speech, in which they expressed their preparedness, and said their only regret was that they were leaving their wives and children. None of them made any reference to the deed for which they paid the penalty. A large crowd was expected and threats had been made to tear down the fence inclosing the scaffold in order that the execution might be made public. Sheriff Stewart was prepared for such an emergency, but set the execution for an early hour in order to prevent trouble.

"If the nomination be tendered to you, would you accept?"

Another Account.
Kaufman, Tex., May 25.—News of the criminal outrage by a negro upon the person of Mrs. Whitworth, the wife of a respectable white farmer, living near Chief, in this county, reached the sheriff's office about 3 p. m. today, and Sheriff Bill Henderson and a posse at once started for the scene. At 9 o'clock tonight a negro was overtaken near Kemp, seven and one-half miles from the scene of outrage, and questioned. He said he had been in the county only three days. He refused to give his name or tell what he had been doing that day. Suddenly he broke away from his questioners and started to run. terrell-terrell-1903-06-05.A3:
WANTED TO BURN.
Negro Who Assaulted a Lady in Kaufman County Had a Close Call.
Kaufman, Tex. May 27.—A criminal
Negro Who Assaulted a Lady in Kaufman County Had a Class Call.

Kaufman, Tex., May 27.—A criminal assault was committed in this county Monday by a negro named John Johnson. Mrs. Charles Whitworth, the wife of a farmer, was the victim. Very soon after the assault was committed a posse of neighbors of the victim started in ed near Kemp about 6 o'clock that night pursuit of the negro and he was arrested after a running fight. The negro was shot several times by members of the posse, and was finally overpowered and taken to Kemp, where he remained until Tuesday morning, when Sheriff Bill Henderson took him in charge and placed him in the county jail. His wounds are serious, his body being filled with small shot and some fingers torn away.

Mrs. Whitworth is the wife of Charlie Whitworth, who lives on the Mason farm, a few miles from Kemp. The negro, John Johnson, had been living in a cabin on the Mason farm for a few weeks. Monday he went to the home of Mr. Whitworth and asked Mrs. Whitworth, who was alone in the house, for a drink of water. While he was in the house he assaulted her. Immediately after the crime was committed Johnson left, but in a short while the news of the crime spread and the entire community shouldered arms and began a diligent search for the criminal, who was overtaken near Kemp, and unceremoniously fired on by the infuriated citizens.

Mrs. Whitworth is still in a critical condition.

Tuesday night Major Roach, commanding the volunteer guard of Dallas, received orders from Austin to go at once to Kaufman with Company E of the Texas Volunteer infantry and the Dallas Field artillery. Soldiers went, but were ordered back, as excitement had quieted down. A mob hauled wood to the court house square with which to burn Johnson. They were prevailed upon not to do so.
terrell-terrell-1903-06-05.A6:
NEGRO RAPIST EXECUTED
Henry Johnson Hung this Afternoon at Kaufman.
Special to Daily Light. Kaufman Ter. May 20
Special to Daily Light.

Kaufman, Tex, May 30, 2:30 p. m.

—Henry Johnson, the negro who criminally assaulted Mrs. John Whitworth, a young married woman, near Kemp Monday evening, expiated his crime on the gallows here this afternoon.

The hanging was public and was witnessed by several thousand people who were here from all parts of the Kaufman and adjoining counties. A special Midland train brought in a large crowd from Ennis.

The gallows were erected in the northeast corner of the court house yard. The Terrell military company was drawn up around the gallows to keep the crowd back and only three or four officers and a negro preacher were on the scaffold with the condemned man. The ceremonies on the scaffold preceding the execution were brief. The negro preacher offered a short prayer and Johnson talked about ten minutes. He was carried up on the scaffold in an arm chair and remained seated in the chair while talking. He had to be held up by officers while the black cap and noose of the rope were adjusted. Promptly at 1 o'clock Sheriff Bill Henderson cut the rope that launched the negro into eternity. The fall was sufficient to break his neck and in four minutes his body was pulseless. Ten minutes after the drop was sprung the negro was pronounced dead. The body will be interred on the county farm.

During the hanging a negro struck at one of John Whitworth's brothers with a large knife, but failed to inflict a blow. A crowd is pursuing him. He lives near Kemp and is regarded as a bad negro.
terrell-terrell-1903-06-05.A7:
RAILROADED TO HIS DEATH. Negro Hanged Legally in Texas Four Days After Committing an Assault.
NEW ORLEANS, May 31.—Henry Johnson was hanged the "Nacogdoches way" at Kaufman, Tex., yesterday, for an assault on Mrs. Wentworth. He was hanged legally within four days of the crime. The case was so railroaded through the courts that there was no time to erect a gallows in the jail. It was impossible under these circumstances to enforce the State law, which forbids hanging in public, and thousands of persons came into Kaufman from the surrounding country and witnessed the hanging.

There was no attempt at violence. The militia, sent to Kaufman to prevent a lynching, were drawn up in the railroad yard and kept the crowd back until the body had been cut down.

The negro confessed that he committed the crime for which he paid the penalty. The law requires that a condemned man shall have thirty days of grace after the sentence of death has been pronounced, but the negro waived this and also waived any appeal to a higher court, as Mrs. Wentworth is lying at the point of death. Great difficulty was encountered in preventing a lynching and only the presence of militia stopped Judge Lynch.

The Nacogdoches way of immediately hanging after sentence of death seems popular in Texas, where it is said to prevent mobbing, rioting and lynching, and also to deter negroes from crime.

AGED NEGRO SHOT DOWN. RICHMOND, Va., Sept. 10.—"Uncle A." Finney, an ex-slave, over ninety years old, who lived in a mountain cabin on the farm of the late James Martin, in Franklin County, was regarded by ignorant people living in the vicinity as being a sorcerer. A few nights ago the old man was called to his door by three men and shot to death. MURPHY KEPT A TAB ON FUSION Tammany Leader Had Underground Connection with the Conference Last Night and Knew What Was Going On. GAVE OUT ORDERS WHILE WAITING FOR THE NEWS. Each Night Young Workers Assemble at Second Avenue and Twentieth Street for Quiet Talks with the Chief.
While the fusion conferrees were fretting and fuming and making speeches last night the man who holds the destinies of Tammany Hall in the hollow of his hand stood against a lamppost at the northwest corner of Twentleth street and Second avenue and smiled and smiled and smiled. There was no fretting or fuming or speechmaking around that corner and it might do some of the fusion leaders good to drop around there and see how the leader of Tammany Hall does his work at night.

It is a quiet corner. There is a big training school for nurses just across the street. An occasional passing trolley car or at long intervals a rushing automobile carrying a merry party to one of the alleged Bohemian east side restaurants is all that serves to break the stillness. Sometimes the rattle of glasses in the saloon over which the Murphy headquarters are located floats faintly through the door.

At 7 o'clock in the evening heavy-jowled young men assemble on the corner from all directions. All are well dressed and most of them wear diamonds. They are the type of young men seen on the race tracks around the betting ring. Beyond a brief greeting few of them talk. They stand around in front of the saloon, on the steps leading to the Anawanda Club or line along the edge of the sidewalk and gaze stolidly into vacancy.

Then Murphy Comes.

In the course of an hour or so there is somewhat of a stir. Former Councilman John Murphy and Alderman Gaffney arrive. John Murphy wears nose glasses these days and looks more like a doctor or professional man than he did when he stood behind the bar of the saloon at Twenty-third street and First avenue. Alderman Gaffney, who has the appearance and movements of an overgrown boy, shakes the hand of everybody.

Murphy goes upstairs. In a moment one of the club attendants comes down and calls one of the young men on the sidewalk. The others look at him curiously as he hurries to obey the summons. Possibly three or four of the waiting men are called upstairs, and then Murphy comes down again, moving from group to group on the sidewalk, talking softly here and there.

Waiting on Murphy.

Finally he appears to have done all his business and stands waiting with the rest. Sometimes the wait is long. The bartenders in the saloon stand behind the bar idle. None of the men go inside while they are waiting for Charles F. Murphy.

Suddenly the leader of Tammany Hall appears. He never comes from the same direction twice in succession. His face is as smooth and as pink as the face of a baby. No one essays to speak to him. His brother John hurries up and talks in an undertone. Then the leader of Tammany Hall takes up his position at the lamppost and brother John sends the waiting men to him.

It is rarely that one of them takes more than a minute or two of Mr. Murphy's time. They do most of the talking. Occasionally he does not open his mouh, simply nodding his head and smiling or scowling as the news seems to affect him.

All Smiles Last Night.

He was all smiles last night. Through some underground system of communication he was kept posted on everything that was being done at the Fusion conference. And after it was all over and the news came that Low had been recommended for renomination the smile grew to a fixture.

"What do you think of Tammany's chances?" he was asked.

"If I didn't think the chances were good I wouldn't say so," he replied.

"Do you think Low is the strongest candidate the Fusionists could select?"

Mr. Murphy thought a long time. Then he said:

"Mr. Low is a great man."
uncle-a-finney-1903-09.A3:
CHARGED WITH SORCERY.
Old Negro Shot to Death by Unknown Men.
Men.

Special Dispatch to The Evening Star.

RICHMOND, Va., September 11.—From Roanoke today comes news of a horrible tragedy in Franklin county, on Nicholson creek, not far from the Patrick county line.

"Uncle A." Finney, an ex-slave, ninety years old, who lived in a mountain cabin, was regarded by the ignorant white people in the vicinity and hundreds of the county darkies as being a sorcerer.

A few nights ago the old man was called to his door by three unknown men and shot to death. Shotguns and rifles were used. One shot passed entirely through the old man's head, killing him instantly. Another tore away the right jaw and a third passed through his neck.

The old man was a trapper of considerable note and spent his time in hunting and occasionally doing chores for the white people of the neighborhood. A few weeks ago Mrs. Mary Holley became ill. She grew worse and her illness baffled the skill of the county physicians. Rumor had it that "Uncle A." had cast a spell over the sick woman. The midnight tragedy shortly afterward occurred. One arrest has been made.
uncle-a-finney-1903-09.A5: AGED NEGRO KILLED. — "Uncle A." Finney, an ex-slave, over 90 years old, who lived in a mountain cabin on the farm of the late James Martin, in Franklin county, was regarded by ignorant people living in the vicinity as being a sorcerer. A few nights ago the old man was called to his door by three unknown men and shot to death. A few weeks ago Mrs. Mary Holley, a white woman, became ill and her illness baffled the skill of the country physicians. Rumor had it that "Uncle A." had cast a spell over the sick woman, and it was not long until this belief became general among the ignorant people of the neighborhood. She grew worse, and nothing could be done to alleviate her sufferings until, according to the reports, the old sorcerer was murdered in his own doorway. Then, for some reason, she began to mend. The neighbors attributed it to the old man's death. His hunting gun was taken. A son of Mrs. Mary Holley was arrested on suspicion of being the guilty party, but was dismissed for want of evidence and has been given his liberty. It is alleged that Holley has made the statement that his mother is gradually recovering her health. Since the tragic death of the old man her entire recovery is now anticipated by her friends. The people of Franklin county are much stirred up over the murder, and it is probable that other arrests will follow.
uncle-a-finney-1903-09.A13:
BARBARISM IN VIRGINIA.
If any one in Eastern Virginia were told that a poor old negro could be murdered in cold blood within the confines of this State, without having committed a crime, without having offended man, woman or child, the person so told would smile at the imagination able to conjure up such a story, and yet, this is just what happened in Franklin county, this State, a few days ago. The story is pathetic enough, sad enough to bring tears to the eye, and barbarous enough, cruel enough to bring the blush of shame to the cheek of every Virginian, since we all must feel the disgrace entailed upon the Commonwealth by such an act as the atrocious murder of the old negro referred to. Peacefully inhabiting his humble log cabin, nearing the line over which he now has passed to meet his God, this old ex-slave, a reminder of that race of black men which existed in the days before the war, and which endeared itself to the South by the love, honesty and fidelity of its people, was shot down at the door of his home by white men, and these white men were Virginians. The reason for this act—the old negro, they say, was a socerer. Is it possible that in Virginia, enlightened by education, by religion and by everything which goes to make up higher civilization, that such a lief, a belief which might not have caused surprise when the Pilgrims and Puritans first inhabited Massachusetts, can still prevail? It seems preposterous, and yet the old negro was murdered forsooth because the ignorant whites in his section of Franklin county believed him a socerer. This story comes from reliable sources, bearing every evidence of truth, and along with it comes the news that the better people of Franklin county will see to it that the brutes who murdered the old man will meet their just reward—at the end of a rope. Such a fate they richly deserve.
uncle-a-finney-1903-09.A14:
Believe in Signs.
A correspondent of the New York Tribune at Crisfield, Maryland, writes: Strange customs and beliefs, which are relics of barbarism, linger among the people, white and colored, along the eastern shores of this state, Virginia, North Carolina and South Carolina. Only one night last week an old negro named Finney was called to his door and riddled with buckshot by men who believed that he was a sorcerer, and had cast a "spell" on a negress named Mary Holley, which had caused her death. Finney was well known as a conjuror and worker of strange things, and there were hundreds, both white and colored, who visited him when they were sick or in trouble, or had lost valuables and wished to find them.

While all the people of this region are full of superstition, some of the people of New Hampshire wear a stocking in the toe of which a potato has been tied, to ward off sore throat; Maine people assert that a nutmeg, pierced and hung on a string around the neck, will prevent sore throat; a double cedar knot is carried in the pocket to prevent rheumatism by Michigan residents; stems from the golden rod are used for the same purpose in Massachusetts; horse chestnuts bring good luck in New Jersey; Irish potatatoes with holes bored through are a cure for rheumatism in New York: turning a shoe upside down under a bed will prevent cramps is the belief of the people of Pennsylvania,

LYNCHING AVERTED
Suspected Murderers of Oneal Jones Escape the Noose.
Holly Springs, Miss., Jan. 20.—The two negroes held as the suspected murderers of Oneal Jones, were carried to Victoria, near the scene of the murder, for a preliminary trial before Justice Benson this morning. They waived examination and were remanded to jail here until circuit court convenes in February. In the presence of more than 2,000 persons, E. H. Wyatt, a negro school teacher, was hanged to a telephone pole and subsequently burned at the stake on the public square in Belleville by a mob of armed citizens last midnight.

The action of the mob was the result of a shooting which occurred late yesterday afternoon in the office of Professor Charles Hertel, Superintendent of Schools of St. Clair County. Hertel and Wyatt had an argument over the issuance of a teachers' certificate. Wyatt shot Hertel through the left breast. He is now at St. Agnes's Infirmary and probably will die.

The mob broke down the doors of the jail with sledge hammers and battering rams. Prior to the forced entrance the quailing negro pleaded for mercy. When the last iron door gave way he fell back on a cot in his cell, helpless from sheer fright.

Immediately the mob rushed upon him. He was beaten, kicked and dragged to the street in an unconscious condition. The nearest telephone pole was his gallows.

Then his clothing was saturated with coal oil and a bonfire started underneath. The flames consumed the clothing, but the nude body, charred and quivering, seemed to accentuate the anger of the infuriated citizens. It was then cut down and more fuel was heaped upon the fire. While the blaze was fiercest Wyatt, all but lifeless, was thrown into the midst of the flames.

It even reached Freeburg, where Professor Hertel lives. Hundreds of farmers from there, armed with shotguns and rifles, hurried to Belleville.

w-t-wyatt-belleville-1903-06-06.A7:
A LYNCHING
IN ILLINOIS

Negro School Teacher
Hooded by Mob.

MURDER WHITE MAN
Body Maltreated After Death Had Come.
The Cause of Shooting Was Refusal of Superintendent Hertel to Re new License of Negro to Teach School.
Belleville, Ill., June 6.—County Superintendent Charles Hertel of St. Clair County was shot and mortally wounded in his office this evening by W. T. Wyatt, a negro school teacher of East St. Louis whose certificate to teach Hertel had refused to rehew.

Wyatt was immediately arrested and taken to jail.

Superintendent Hertel was removed to a hospital where the physicians probed for the bullet, but they stated that there was no chance for his recovery. Hertel said Wyatt had shot him because of his refusal to renew a certificate for teaching. A young man of the name of Fielder was in the office when the shooting occurred. He grappled with Wyatt who inflicted on him a scalp wound with the butt of his revolver. A passing policeman entered the room and arrested the negro. He was hurled to the county jail and the jail was surrounded with policemen as it was feared a mob might form. A couple of hours passed when suddenly a mob appeared before the jail and forced an entrance to Wayatt's cell, despite the protests of the mayor and chief of police. Securing the prisoner, the mob dragged him out and hanged him to a telephone pole in the public square next to the court house. Wyatt asserted that the shooting was a result of a political grudge. When Wyatt was pronounced dead the body was kicked about and then buried.
w-t-wyatt-belleville-1903-06-06.A13:
A Fiendish Illinois Atrocity.
All the best people in Belleville, Ill., were present Saturday at the lynching of a negro. Women attended with their children; and small boys, from points of advantageous view, announced to the mob the progress of events as the leaders slowly hammered down doors between themselves and the wretched negro. Nothing was done to stay the mob, except that the mayor made a speech which unfortunately had the effect of inflaming the mob's blood passion. The negro was burned after he had been stunned and choked. The crowd is described as very orderly and chiefly composed of spectators, the actual lynching being done by about fifteen unmasked men, but the dispatch adds that there will be no arrests because the murderers cannot be identified. All this is not in Kishinef or in the Philippines or in Africa, but in the great, populous and powerful state of Illinois. It is up to the state authorities to force an investigation of this dreadful business, and assert the law's rightful monopoly of public justice.

The officials at Belleville counseled nothing more than passive resistance to the mob on the ground that force would anger the man-hunters. One of these days some sheriff will stand by his post of duty, anger the mob with an offer of force for force and when the crisis comes will shoot with deadly aim. The sheriff who will set a good example to all other sheriffs and establish a monitory record for mobs, by shooting to kill, will do much to end the rule of mob law. It would be almost enough to elect to the sheriff's office men known to be fearless and determined. It is a nice sport to hunt a lone, defenseless prisoner out of a jail while the officials look on, and quite another thing to conduct the hunt with the chances favorable to the hunter being potted himself.

By the way, Sheriff Castles of Montrose county, Wisconsin, would doubtless have inflicted summary punishment on a lynching mob at Tomah and Sparta last week if the mob had dared to carry out its threats. Like a man of duty and action he rescued his prisoner from the mob at Tomah with the aid of a dozen rifle carrying deputies and took him to Sparta, where another mob snarled around the jail but dared not strike in view of the force that stood ready to do a little legal killing if the mob had tried to lynch the prisoner. Belleville needs a Castles, and so do hundreds of counties in the United States. If there were more shooting sheriffs, there would be fewer hanging mobs.

THE OUTRAGEOUS WHITES
Citizens assembled in groups at every corner to discuss the lynching. Strangers were told in gruesome detail of the victim's shrieks for mercy, at his writhing at the dangling end of the rope, and how the flames flared up and licked at the foot of the victim, but this did not satisfy the mob, and another and larger fire was started nearby. When it had begun burning briskly the Negro, still half alive, was taken down, and after being covered with coal oil was cast into the fire. Groans of pain were heard from the half roasted victim of the mob and these served further to infuriate his torturers. They set upon him with clubs and beat the burning body almost to pieces, and not until every sign of life had departed did they desist and permit the flames to devour the body. The pastors of the Belleville churches without exception denounced the lynching. The Rev. Dr. John Gallagher of the Presbyterian church was exceptionally severe, declaring the act of the mob as deliberate and premeditated murder. While public sentiment is apparently with the mob, signs of a revolusion of feeling are already noticeable. Business men and leading citizens are beginning to realize the stigma that has been cast upon the fame of the city. It is now declared that the Negro was not lynched by citizens of Belleville, but by farmers from the neighborhoods of Freeburg and Turkey Hill, where Supt Hertel resides. State Attorney Farmer stated this afternoon that he would request the court to call an extra session of the grand jury to thoroughly investigate the lynching. He claims to have incriminative evidence against certain farmers of, Freeburg and Turkey Hill. He also declares he will implicate certain citizens of Belleville. WIDOW CLAIMS CHARRED BODY. w-t-wyatt-belleville-1903-06-06.A36:
The Grand Old State Again Disgraced —This Time an Educated Afro- American and a Good Citizen Is the Victim.
Belville, Ill.-The anti-Negro sentiment here is running high, as a result of the lynching and burning of David J. Wyatt, the Afro-American teacher, a few hours after he had shot and wounded Chas. Hertel, superintendent of the St. Clair county schools. The 500 Afro-American residents of this city very properly refuse to heed a warning to leave town. Wyatt was 35 years of age, highly educated and a splendid citizen. He had been teaching school in St. Clair county for the last ten years. He leaves a wife and four children. His friends, both here and in all parts of St. Clair county, are threatening retribution. We sincerely trust they will carry out their threat.

Superintendent Hertel is still alive. The shooting of Superintendent Hertel, from what we learn, was entirely justified. Fully 10,000 strangers visited the Public square Sunday and viewed the scene of the lynching. Only the charred telephone pole and a few bits of unconsumed flesh of the unfortunate man remained for their view. The pastors of the Belleville churches without exception denounced the lynching.

Should Quiet The South Halers.
The horriable details of the lynching and burning alive of a negro at Bellaville, in the State of Illinois, sent out by the Associated Press and printed in these columns yesterday morning, ought to quiet the South haters of Chicago, as well as those of New England, at least for a while. The negro in this case had quarreled with and killed a county superintendent of education. The Illinois mob hanged him awhile and then burned him to death. Nothing like it in all its shocking details has occurred in the South, even when the victim had been lynched to avenge crimes against defenseless women and children. The Illinois incident ought to give the country a new vision of the race question.—Indianapolis Sentinel.

GO AND GET A GUN.
Negro Preacher's Advice to His Race on the Subject of Lynchings.
CHICAGO, June 24.—The Rev. C. H. Thomas, pastor of a negro church in Belleville, Ill., evoked tumults of applause last night at a meeting held in Quinn Chapel to denounce the recent burning of David B. Wyatt by a Belleville mob. The preacher said:

"My Master said, 'If there is no sword here sell your coat and get one.' If lynching and burning do not cease I say to every black man: Sell your coat and get a gun." He then denounced Gov. Yates for failing to interfere.
w-t-wyatt-belleville-1903-06-06.A116:
MAYOR KERN EXPLAINS ACTION.
Statement From the Chief Executive of Belleville, Illinois.

In answers to criticisms of his action in not using more forcible means to disperse the mob which lynched the negro, Wyatt, at Belleville, Ill., on the night of June 6, Mayor Kern said:

"It is true that I requested the officers not to use their guns. I did so after careful reflection. I was convinced in my judgment that to do so would not stop the citizens in their determination to get Wyatt, but that such a course simply would fan the flame of their insane fury. I was convinced that to do so would precipitate a battle. I was convinced that many citizens would be killed or maimed in the encounter.

"The officers did their full duty. They arrested the assasin. They locked him up in one of the strongest and most modern jails in this or any other country. They exhausted their possibilities in defending the prisoner. They could not be asked to kill and lay down their own lives to save a murderer. The men actually on the ground were the best judges of the critical situation.

"You ask me who is to blame for the lynching. The negro, Wyatt, who came into this community armed and with murder in his craven heart is to blame for it. The negro, Wyatt, who

tried to murder the county superintendent of schools is to blame for it first and last.

"I don't approve of mob law. I do not wish to be understood to condone the offense of the mob. But there was a reason for the fury which burst forth. Murders have been too frequent in our county of late.

"The assault on Mr. Hertel was singularly atrocious in its nature. It was Wyatt who disturbed the peace of our community. It was he who fired the shot which felled Hertel. He and he alone was to blame for the irregular execution of himself. He suffered the consequence of his own cowardly deed."

Robuked the Trumpeter.

When Lord Wolseley was commander in chief of the British military forces he went to inspect a garrison in the south of Ireland, the chief officer of which was addicted to sulphurous language. During the interview the colonel ordered that the trumpeter sound the "charge," but unfortunately the man blew the "retreat" instead. The colonel was about to let loose a volley of verbal fireworks when he remembered Lord Wolseley was within hearing. For a moment it looked as though he might explode, but he found temporary relief in rearing at the man. "Oh, you naughty, naughty trumpeter." Later in the day he made up for this moderation by blasting the offender all over the barracks.

HAPPENINGS IN EAST SIDE CITIES AND TOWNS TEN GIVE BOND ON RIOT CHARGE. Bail Fixed at $200 Against Men Accused of Being Implicated in Lynching of Negro. MORE ARRESTS TO FOLLOW. All Declare They Had Nothing to Do With Death of Wyatt and Say They Were Disinterested Spectators. MEN ARRESTED ON CHARGE OF BEING IM- PLICATED IN LYNCHING. Eugene Hay, bookkeeper. George Schopp, carpenter. William Deimling, molder. Henry Harszy, teamster. Albert Weber, molder. John Edelderf, plumber. Julius Schwind, blacksmith. Frank Schilling, nickelplater. Mathew Weiss, coal miner. John Weicking, coal miner.
Ten citizens of Belleville, indicted by the Grand Jury on charges of rioting in connection with the lynching of the negro David S. Wyatt on Saturday night, June 6. were arrested yesterday by Deputy Klamm of Belleville, and were later released on $200 bond each.

Several spent a couple of hours each in jail before their friends secured surety for their release. It is understood that several more will be arrested to-day.

Among the citizens charged with being implicated in the lynching is Eugene Hay, nephew of County Judge John B. Hay, and one of the prominent young business and society men of Belleville.

Mr. Hay heard that he had been indicted and hurried to the Sheriff's office early yesterday morning and gave himself up. Ernest Wangelin of the Crescent Nail Mill went on his bond. Mr. Hay thought at first that the indictment was a joke, and says that he will have no difficulty in proving that he did not participate in the riot and lynching.

George Schopp, a carpenter, was the next arrested. He declared that he had nothing to do with the lynching, although he was in the crowd.

William Diemling, a molder, denied all complicity in the riot, and declares that a mistake was made in indicting him.

Henry Harszy, a teamster, admitted having been in the jail prior to the lynching, but said that he had nothing to do with the lynching and was merely a spectator. He says that he saw the negro dragged from his cell and also saw him hanged on the public square, but that he was a disinterested spectator during the proceeding.

Albert Weber, a molder, was arrested while eating dinner at his home. He admitted being in the crowd, but denied participating in the lynching.

John Edeldorf, a plumber, declared that some one was putting up a joke on him when the Deputy Sheriff read a caplas to him placing him under arrest for complicity in the lynching. Edeldorf said that he was around the jail early in the evening, when there was some talk of lynching the negro, but that he then purposely left and went to a saloon in another part of the town, where he spent the evening playing pool.

Julius Schwind, a blacksmith of East Main street, objected to being arrested by Deputy Sheriff Klamm, but finally decided that he had better submit, and accompanied the deputy to the jail.

Schwind is a member of a fire company and says that when the fire company was called out to disperse the crowd he was with them and did his duty. He denies being in the mob.

will-pettiford-bellevue-1903-05.A1:
MOB READY WITH ROPE
Negro Murderers in Jail at Fremont, O., in Danger of Being Lynched.
Fremont, O., May 9.—A serious conflict, the outcome of labor troubles in this city, occurred here late tonight. Otto Mischke, 20 years old, was shot and killed and Albert Gummell fatally wounded, the shooting being done by a gang of colored nonunion men, three of whom are now in jail. The police are searching for the others.

A party had taken place at the Gummell home, and as the guests were homeward bound they met a crowd of colored men. Remarks passed at which the negroes took offense and the shooting followed, the colored men starting the shooting.

Albert Gummell was shot in the leg and body, and his son, R. C. Gummell, was shot in the leg.

Otto Mischke, who came to the rescue, was shot through the heart and instantly killed.

The police soon arrested three colored men, all claiming Cleveland as their home. Although late when the murder was committed the news soon spread, and great excitement was created, and a mob was soon formed and started for the jail. All but three of the negroes in the party escaped.

William Kimbro is the man who is believed to have killed Mischke, he having partially made a confession, it is said.

Revolvers which had recently been discharged and reloaded were found on the persons of the three arrested negroes.

Cleveland, May 10. 2:10 a.m.—A bulletin just received from Fremont says the mob still surrounds the jail, clamoring for the prisoners. A false alarm of fire has been turned in with the hope of scattering the crowd.

The police are using every effort to prevent the prisoners falling into the hands of the mob, and at this hour express the hope of being able to do so.
will-pettiford-bellevue-1903-05.A3:
WAS NO LYNCHING.
Sheriff at Fremont Succeeded in Averting It. Fremont. O. May 10-Mob violence
Sheriff at Fremont Succeeded in Averting It.

Fremont, O., May 10.—Mob violence, which was threatened in this city last night as the result of the alleged killing of Otto Mischke by one of three negroes, subsided at 4 o'clock this morning. The three negroes who are charged with the crime are securely locked in the county jail at Norwalk, and the excitement that was rampant for several hours last night has about subsided.

From 1 o'clock until 4 o'clock Sunday morning, the jail building was surrounded by the angry crowd calling upon Sheriff Mason to deliver the prisoners. For an hour or more the sheriff stood on the front steps of his residence and admonished the threatening crowd to be careful and quiet, and not commit an act that would forever shame Fremont in the eyes of the world. Sheriff Mason said he had taken an oath to do his official duty, and do it he would, and he said he would shoot the first man who made an attempt to break down the jail door and enter the building.

For fear of further trouble during the day and to-night, Mayor Engler ordered every saloon in the city closed.

The negroes gave their names as Wheeler Kimbro, Walter Stratton and Lorenzo Martin. Martin and Stratton had loaded revolvers in their possession.

To-day's story of the tragedy is to the effect that the negroes who were in the street were offended at a question of Mrs. Albert Gommel as to who they were. Mrs. Gommel was on her way home with her husband and children. Mische, the victim of the bullet, was living at the Gommel House, which was in the vicinity of the affray, and when he came to the door to see what the loud talk was about, a bullet struck him in the stomach, inflicting a fatal wound.
will-pettiford-bellevue-1903-05.A5:
SHOT IN A RACE CLASH.
White Man Killed and Another Wounded in Fremont, Ohio.
FREMONT, Ohio, May 10.—As a result of a clash between some negroes and whites here about midnight last night, Otto Miscke, white, is dead, and Gilbert Gommell, white, received a bullet in his thigh. Three negroes, Wheeler Kimber, Lorenzo Martin and Walter Shatton, are in jail charged with murder.

Ralph Gommell was going home from a party at his father's house, accompanied by his wife and baby. As he passed a crowd of negroes he made a remark, to which they replied. Gommell threw a stone, striking Kimber on the head.

The negroes then drew revolvers and began firing. Albert Gommell, father of Ralph, and Otto Miscke ran out of the house. Miscke received a bullet in his side and staggered back into the house, falling dead at the door, and Gommell received a bullet in the thigh.

The police were summoned and arrested the negroes, who had taken refuge in a house. When the news of the killing became known, a crowd of 200 men went to the jail and demanded the men. Not having a leader, the crowd dispersed. This afternoon the men were taken to Newark jail for safety.

will-pettiford-bellevue-1903-05.A14:
THE FREMONT RIOT
So many conflicting stories have been sent broadcast over the country relative to the riot in Fremont, O., last Saturday night, resultant from a strike of the employees of the Clauss shear works, that it is about time for the truth to have a hearing. The facts are, that a number of Afro-Americans from Cleveland and other northern Ohio points were employed to take strikers' places. Some did not know that this was to be the case until almost on their arrival in Fremont. Others were made acquainted with the situation before arrival. As is usually the case, a mob consisting of strikers and sympathizers assaulted three young Afro-Americans by the names of Stratton, Kimbro and Martin, injuring severely at least one of them. They retaliated, shooting into the crowd and killing at least one striker and injuring others. This, of course, was in self-defense, because their lives were being jeopardized. As is usually the case, the Afro-Americans were arrested and taken to the jail at Norwalk, O., after a very weak attempt was made by two or three foolish admirers of the southern way of doing such things—lynching. They did not tarry long near the Fremont jail, because the sheriff told them in very plain language that he would kill anyone who approached any nearer the jail door. This, of course, settled the matter as far as the cowards were concerned. The following dispatches to the daily papers of Wednesday and Thursday are self-explanatory: Norwalk, O., May 12.—The case of Stratton, Kimbro and Martin, the three young colored men brought to Norwalk from Fremont Sunday, will be investigated by the Sandusky county grand jury to-morrow. This plan will obviate the necessity of taking the prisoners to Fremont for a preliminary examination before a magistrate and consequently they will probably be kept in jail in Norwalk until they are placed on trial in the common pleas court. Their attorneys will probably ask for a change of venue, so that it is probable that the trials will take place in Huron county. The three prisoners, acting upon the advice of their attorneys, refuse to talk about the shooting affair in Fremont, merely saying that the published accounts are untrue, that the "other side" was more to blame than they were and that the truth will become known at the proper time. Fremont, O., May 13.—A country churchyard could not have been more quiet or more orderly than Fremont was to-day. The militia was not needed, there being no disturbances. No demonstration was made near the Clauss factory other than the assembling of a large crowd expecting to see trouble when the management attempted to start the works. No attempt was made by sympathizers, either by word or force, to prevent any man who desired from entering the factory. Only a few entered, not sufficient to operate the works. Strikers Indicted for Murder.
FREMONT, O., May 18.—Indictments for murder were returned this afternoon by the grand jury against Wheeler Kimbro, Lorenzo Martin, Walter Stratton, Richard Pettiford and William Pettiford, all colored. They are charged with the murder of Otto Mischke, who was killed by a bullet wound in the stomach. The Pettifords are named as accessories to the crime in that they were advisers.

Dear Editor: In behalf of my two friendly colleagues, Walter Stratton and Lorenzo Martin, allow me to thank you for your kindness and true friendship to us in your paper. will-smith-memphis-1903-08-29.A1:
IN DARKEST MEMPHIS.
The Manner in Which a Tennessee Policeman Enforces the Law.
Memphis Commercial Appeal.

Life in this community is cheap; the life of a negro so valueless that it is freely taken without fear of future punishment in this world. Yesterday morning a negro died at the City Hospital from a wound inflicted by Lewis G. Slaughter, a merchant at 1077 Walker avenue, who had been deputized by Patrolman A. S. Boyles to guard the prisoner while he went after his uniform. The negro was shot down in cold blood, apparently without justification, and after the manner of a dog. This is the testimony of eye witnesses, women of highest respectability and virtue, who were present when the tragedy was enacted. Those implicated give another version; they always do in such cases.

From the news story of the crime as published in the Commercial Appeal, this negro, who is said to have been harmless and inoffensive, was hawking chickens in that neighborhood. Patrolman Boyles saw him, and with his keen Foxy Quiller brain and eye discovered in him a thief who was trying to dispose of his pilfered wares. Suspending work on a house he was building, Patrolman Boyles accosted the negro, called him a thief, rushed to his house, secured his pistol, and then came back and arrested him. "I took the negro to Slaughter's grocery," said Patrolman Boyles in an interview, "and asked Mr. Slaughter to watch him until I could go back home and get on my uniform. I handed my pistol to Slaughter as I went out and remarked: 'If this man tries to get away from you, kill him.'" Continuing his narrative Patrolman Boyles says:

"A few minutes after I left the negro
kill him." Continuing his narrative Patrolman Boyles says:

"A few minutes after I left the negro jumped up and made a break for the door. Slaughter took my injunction to shoot him literally and fired. The first shot brought the man down."

This is the story of an officer who reported to acting Chief of Police Perry that he had killed the negro because he had broken away from him in an effort to escape. It was very magnanimous in Patrolman Boyles to take upon himself the sins of another. Such events are so rare that each is a classic, and Boyles and Slaughter now take their positions on pedestals in the hall at the opposite end of the shade on which fronts that gallery filled with heroes and martyrs, chief among which are Damon and Pythias. But how much credence is to be placed in the words of an officer, sworn to his duty, clothed with the ring of authority and invested with the majesty of the law, who deliberately makes a false statement to his chief? "I stated that I shot the negro," said he, "because I considered myself as much responsible as if I had done it." Here is a solemn truth! Patrolman Boyles is responsible for this crime. Who gave him power of attorney to deputize Lewis G. Slaughter to guard his prisoner, and "kill him if he tries to get away?" Was the negro so obstreperous, so powerful, so pugnacious that Patrolman Boyles needed assistance? Why could not Patrolman Boyles have taken the negro to his home, if it was necessary for him to get on his uniform? Why did not Patrolman Boyles call the patrol wagon and send the negro to the station? If there ever was a case in which more ignorance, more carelessness and more laxity of law was evidenced than this, the records do not disclose it. Patrolman Boyles evidenced all the deficiencies which enter into the make-up of a thoroughly inefficient and incompetent police officer. That he thought the taking of human life a small matter is fully shown by this brief but telling dialogue, which occurred between Patrolman Boyles and Slaughter just after the killing:

"Well, you got him, didn't you?" said Boyles.

"If I didn't, I almost," replied Slaughter with a smile.

The more one reflects on this affair the greater the indignation that burns within him. This negro was a harmless creature, perhaps from the rural districts, who would naturally become confused when accosted by a policeman and accused, as he was in this instance, of being a thief and having the goods on him. The sight of a pistol would add to his terror, and his first impulse would be to flee from his captor. He was docile and easily taken, and had he been a bad man with a criminal record, as Patrolman Boyles asserts, he would not have allowed himself to have been arrested, but would have evaded the unarmed officer. But he meekly submitted to arrest, waiting for the officer to get his pistol from the house, and walked submissively to Slaughter's store. Here he was terrorized by the command to kill him, and had he made a break for liberty it would have been a natural consequence of the circumstances. But bystanders asseverate that he did not run, and that he was murdered in cold blood. The report further states that a small boy was in the track of the bullet, which would have killed him had it not struck the negro first.

Slaughter is said to be "an aged man, and an ex-Confederate soldier." Does this palliate his offense? Does the record of honorable service in the Confederate army license a man to violate the supreme command of the Almighty? Worth makes the man, not a war record and the clothes he wears. Because Slaughter's locks are rimy with age, and because he wore the gray does not mitigate his offense.

Acting Chief of Police Perry is quoted as saying that Slaughter will not be arrested, and it is inferred that Patrolman Boyles will resume his beat and continue the work on his house. If this is the denouement, then is justice a misnomer in this city. The coroner should probe this matter to the bottom, and the death of this low-browed, unthinking and unoffending negro should be avenged by the law. It must not be said in this community that the life of even the humblest citizen can be taken with impunity.

NEGRO DIES IN HOSPITAL AFTER HAVING RECEIVED FATAL INJURIES.
William Sm'th, An Invollensive Negro Shot Down In Cold Blood By A Butcher At The Instigation Of Policeman Who Told Him To Shoot In Case The Negro Attempted To Run.—Commercial Appeal Takes Up The Case And Makes An Investigation Of The Facts. Memphis, Tenn., Sept. 3.—William Smith, the Negro, who was shot by Lewis G. Slaughter, a groceryman on Walker avenue, died yesterday morning about 11 o'clock, at the city hospital, where he had been taken after receiving hff fatal injuries. The shooting of the Negro, which took place early Saturday morning, has aroused considerable indignation on account of the very apparent cruelty and inhumanity shown in the killing. After the shooting had taken place The Commercial Appeal went to the bottom of the case and probed all of the facts connected with it. A post mortem statement was obtained from the dying Negro, which was printed exclusively in that paper, and which corroborated completely the statements given out by eye witnesses to the tragedy. It was sutured in this story that the Negro, Smith, had been shot in front of the grocery and barroom of Lewis G. Slaughter, at 1077 Walker avenue. The Negro had been in the vicinity of the place selling chickens and had been placed under arrest by Patrolman Boyles who was off duty at the time. After the Negro had been placed under arrest Boyles had turned him over to the grocerman and had given the latter his gun with the injunction to kill the Negro if he attempted to escape. The Negro was fatally shot by Slaughter. Eye witnesses state that the shooting was unprovoked. They state further that a child was standing in range of the deadly bullet, and was knocked down by the wounded man as he rolled bleeding from the steps. They report a cold and cruel colloquijet between Boyles and Slaughter over the prostrate body. Will Smith was taken to the city hospital. Boyles went to the police station and reported to his superior officers that he himself had done the shooting. He said nothing of having deputized Slaughter to guard the Negro until after the publication in The Commercial Appeal exposing the facts in connection with the tragedy. Then he authorized a statement in an afternoon paper admitting that Slaughter fired the fatal shot, and claiming that his deputy had "taken literally" his injunction to "kill the Negro if

Capt. O. H. Perry, who is acting chief of police at the present time, said yesterday that no action had as yet been taken by the department toward arresting any one for the killing of Smith. He said that the result of the coroner's inquest would be awaited before the department would take any move in the matter.

william-dorsey-peach-bottom-1903-08-11.A1:
LYNCHINGS AVERTED.
The town of Peach Bottom, near York, Pa., had a small race war Tuesday in which William Dorsey, a negro, was shot. Dorsey and another colored man, Charles Haywood, were denied drinks at John T. Moore's hotel. This angered the men, and they assaulted Moore with revolvers and knives. He procured a shotgun and filled Dorsey's hip and back with shot. The two negroes, who are desperate characters, and who have been terrorizing the lower end of the county for several months, narrowly escaped lynching when the news of their conduct spread, a mob having been formed to administer lynch law. The legal authorities captured the negroes, however, and succeeded in carrying them to York, where they were placed in jail.

Eight negroes were arrested for an attempted criminal assault on Mrs. Hart, a white woman, at Whitesboro, Texas, yesterday. Seven were released and the eighth man was held for identification. A mob appeared at the jail last night, took the negro and hanged him to a tree nearby. Before he became unconscious officers appeared and rescued the negro and hurried him to Sherman for safe-keeping. The mob is gathering to pursue the prisoner, and it is said other communities will join the mob.
william-dorsey-peach-bottom-1903-08-11.A3:
QUICK OPERATION OF LAW.
Man Arrested, Tried and Sentenced In a Day.
Man Arrested, Tried and Sentenced In a Day.
York, Pa., Aug. 31.—Quick operation of the law in York county was demonstrated in the case of Charles A. Forward, who, with William Dorsey, was charged with assault and battery with intent to kill and carrying concealed deadly weapons.
These charges were preferred by John T. Moore of Peach Bottom, and J. Street and William Whitehead, two men from Maryland. Forward was arrested Thursday morning, heard by an alderman and his case sent to court.
Friday both men were found guilty. Each was sentenced to four years in the Eastern penitentiary. Forward's whole experience with the law covered less than 24 hours.

william-noblett-farmington-1903-10.A2:
WILL PUNISH WHITE CAPPERS.
Marshall County Grand Jury Indicts Men Suspected of Beating Up Farmington Negroes.
Special to the Herald.
Lewisburg, Nov. 18
Special to the Herald.

Lewisburg, Nov. 18.—Several weeks ago this county was stirred up over a whitecap raid near Farmington, and as a result of which a negro, William Noblett, and his wife were badly beaten. The scene of the raid was near the line between Marshall and Bedford counties and shortly thereafter seven men were placed under arrest, under suspicion of being implicated in the outrage. They are Hill Perryman, Bose Erwin, George, Claud and Will Cheves and Bob and Rose Darnall, and all of them are residents of the Eighteenth district of Bedford county. The men were given a preliminary hearing at the time, before a magistate at Farmington, and were released.

The Grand Jury took hold of the matter and this morning returned indictments against all of the suspects. A hearing of the case has been set for Friday and Gov. Frazier has appointed C. A. Armstrong to assist Attorney General Falkner in the prosecution.
william-noblett-farmington-1903-10.A4: Jim Glasscock, Bob Darnell, Rose Darnell and George and Will Chives were sentenced to jail for four months each at Lewisburg for whitecapping.

Another Disastrous Incendiary Fire.
Once again the dirty, villainous work of the fire bug has brought destruction and ruin to our otherwise quiet and prosperous town, and destroyed two of the largest and most up-to date business houses in this part of the state. The residents of our town were awakened on Friday morning at 5 o'clock by the fire alarm, and responding readily, found the magnificent brick dry goods store of Mr. C. Schaefer enwrap in flames from within, and the fiery tongues licking out angrily from every opening. To save any of the contents of this store was impossible, and no effort was made. Attention was then turned to removing the goods from the grocery store of M. W. Brown, a respected colored merchant of our town, and also from the Hardware store of Mr. G. A. Wettlin; some of these goods were saved—both of which were in frame buildings. The losses are approximately as follows:

C. Schaefer's loss $32,000.
Insurance, 12,000.
G. A Wettlin, loss 10,000.
Insurance, 4,000.
M. W. Brown, loss 300.

To add to the seriousness of the conflagration it will be remembered that on Nov. 2nd 1898, the store of Mr. Schaefer was destroyed by fire with a loss of $15,000, and on April 14, 1900, Mr. Wettlin's store was destroyed with a loss of $9,000 and he sustained losses in the fire in 1899. Brown also burned out at a previous fire.

To read this account makes the blood boil, and everything should and will be done to apprehend the guilty party, or parties. A subscription list, which we give below was raised in a short time, as a reward for the arrest and conviction of the perpetrator of this heinous crime. While this reward will be an incentive to ferret out the guilty ones, every good citizen of our county will be active in leading aid in any way whereby the guilty may be brought to justice. We are unable to give a more lengthy account in this issue. In conclusion we wish to ask where was the night watchman, who is paid to guard the town at night. Had he been on his beat there is a possibility that the fire would have been discovered in ample time to extinguish it.
